Research from the Sumeru Akademiya suggests the technology may predate them: Jazari reports that Azosite power systems were probably in widespread use long before the first ruin machine was built in ancient Khaenri'ah, so the Khaenri'ahns need not have invented it.

Later Khaenri'ahn engineers found more effective power sources, including Abyssal energy, and these gradually replaced Azosite systems. The change shows in the machines: early ruin machines carry Azosite backup power, later ones do not. Jazari reads this as a transition period in which the Khaenri'ahns had not yet mastered Abyssal energy and kept Azosite as a safety net. Worn notes in the ruins call the factory Hangeh Afrasiyab the last workshop in the kingdom with a complete Azosite-powered system, after the smelting furnace of the Royal Machine Workshop "Gnade" was officially abandoned. They say its efficiency problems were hard to solve and that even small mass-produced machines such as Field Tillers found a power core more convenient. The author predicted the workshop would soon close too, and lamented that people are shortsighted about technology.

Another ruin note, an unfinished letter to a marshal of the kingdom, asks that some machinery built to the "old standard" be kept under his ministry's care so that it might spark future generations to explore technology by their own will. Whether the request was granted is not recorded.

Usage sites: Hangeh Afrasiyab, an abandoned underground factory in Gavireh Lajavard (Sumeru), was where Azosite was processed; a sealed gate to Khaenri'ah lies in its depths. In the quest "As the Khvarena's Light Shows," the Traveler and companions retrieved a Great Song of Khvarena there.

Madinat al-Nuhas is named as a large weapons-testing facility powered by Azosite. The Khaenri'ahn ruins beneath Gavireh Lajavard and the Realm of Farakhkert hold the notes that explain the process, and the Mysterious Energy Block appears in the quest "As the Khvarena's Light Shows: Nirodha."

Rene observations: Around the time of the cataclysm, Rene, a researcher from Fontaine, visited Hangeh Afrasiyab and studied Azosite. He judged it convenient, stable and safe, yet lacking "will" because it is pure elemental force, comparing the gap to that between a Hydro Slime and an Oceanid. He thought the Khaenri'ahns' use of the Abyss too primitive, steering their "evolution" in an uncontrollable direction. He also wondered whether Khvarena, which can reverse Abyssal influence, might be smelted by the Azosite method; he thought a true perpetual energy source of the kind the Khaenri'ahns idealised might result, and that learning the origin of Amrita, which he thought might be influencing Khvarena, could point to a way to raise the mortal to "supreme purity." These are speculations, not demonstrated results.

Limits: Azosite is pure elemental energy and so obeys the rules of elemental energy; it has no will of its own and sits beneath Abyssal power in the order of rules. Canon shows it only as Khaenri'ahn-era infrastructure and notes, not as a power anyone wields today.

Azosite is not a substitute for a Vision, a Gnosis or an Archon's Authority, and canon never shows it granting abilities to a person. Do not treat it as a separate sixth kind of element.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat Azosite as old industrial infrastructure. Scenes can feature sealed smelting furnaces, stacked Energy Blocks, dim Ruin Golems on backup power, and worn engineers' notes. Scholars in Sumeru can plausibly discuss it as a curiosity from the Khaenri'ahn ruins.

A character who has read Rene's or Jazari's findings can cite them, with the caveats above. Ordinary people do not know the term; it is mostly known to scholars of Khaenri'ah and Akademiya researchers.

39.content: Energy Blocks are solid, refined Azosite used to fuel the backup power systems of Ruin Golems. The Mysterious Energy Block is a quest item from "As the Khvarena's Light Shows: Nirodha," described as a block of refined Azosite formed by condensing pure elemental energy for large-scale power systems. The wiki also lists a Lost Energy Block as another form of Azosite.

40.content: An abandoned underground factory in Gavireh Lajavard where the Khaenri'ahns processed Azosite, described in notes as the last workshop in the kingdom with an entirely Azosite-powered system. A sealed gate to Khaenri'ah lies within, and the Traveler recovered a Great Song of Khvarena there in the quest "As the Khvarena's Light Shows."

41.content:
Bloom (also: Bloom reaction, Dendro Core, Dendro Cores, Bountiful Core, Bountiful Cores): Bloom is what happens when Dendro and Hydro meet on a target, in either order. The result is a Dendro Core: a small bud-like object that sits on the field for a few seconds and then bursts in a spray of Dendro damage around it. It arrived in Version 3.0 with the Dendro element.

A Dendro Core can also be hit with a third element before it bursts. Pyro turns it into Burgeon, a bigger blast. Electro turns it into Hyperbloom, a homing projectile (Sprawling Shot). Both are summarised below and have their own entries.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Bloom is shown in tutorials and combat, not discussed by characters in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction: a scene may borrow its look (a seed forming from water and verdant energy) but should not present a named in-world law.

Related setting: Dendro is the element associated with Sumeru. The wiki also notes that creatures made of Dendro, the Tri-Lakshana creatures, react with Hydro and Electro as Bloom and Quicken.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Dendro applied to a Hydro-affected target, or Hydro applied to a Dendro-affected one, creates a Dendro Core. It lasts up to 6 seconds. If it expires while the character who made it is still in the party and alive, it explodes for area Dendro damage in a 5 m radius, hurting enemies and players alike. Otherwise it simply disappears.

- At most 5 Dendro Cores exist at once; making a sixth makes the oldest expire immediately.
- Burgeon: Pyro on a Dendro Core consumes it and causes a larger Dendro explosion, also in a 5 m radius, to enemies and players.
- Hyperbloom: Electro on a Dendro Core turns it into a Sprawling Shot that homes in on the closest enemy and hits for increased Dendro area damage in a 1 m radius. If an enemy or the environment triggers it, it homes on the closest ally instead.
- Damage to players from every Bloom-related reaction is 2% of what the same reaction deals to enemies, whoever triggers it.
- Burgeon and Hyperbloom may be triggered by a different party from the one that made the Core, including the environment, and they scale with the stats of whoever applied the Pyro or Electro.

- Bountiful Cores: certain character abilities and event buffs make Bloom produce Bountiful Cores instead. These explode 0.4 seconds after creation in a 6.5 m radius, again dealing 2% to players. Burgeon and Hyperbloom cannot be triggered on them, and they share the limit of 5 with ordinary Dendro Cores.
- Damage limit: one target can take only 2 instances of damage from each Bloom-related reaction per source every 0.5 seconds. Reactions triggered by one character do not share this limit with another's, and Dendro Core and Bountiful Core explosions are counted separately.
- Damage is Transformative: it comes from the triggering character's level and Elemental Mastery, and the wiki gives separate tables for Bloom and for Burgeon/Hyperbloom.
- Trivia from the wiki: the Lea Lotus Lamp made by the Dendro Traveler's Elemental Burst counts as a Hyperbloom target when an enemy or the environment triggers the reaction.

Several talents, constellations and artifact sets raise Bloom, Burgeon or Hyperbloom damage, make Dendro Cores burst at once, let these reactions deal critical hits, or add flat base damage; the wiki keeps them in category tables, which this entry does not copy.

Lunar bloom: Lunar-Bloom (own entry) is the Moonsign form of Bloom, which the wiki records as introduced in Version Luna I. It needs a party member with a qualifying Moonsign Benediction passive, so it is not available to every team. According to the wiki it deals no damage itself; damage comes only through character talents and constellations. Triggering it grants the player Verdant Dew, one every 2.5 seconds for up to 3, and the Dew persists across party changes, teleports, domains, daily resets and game sessions.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Bloom as a bud or seed of green energy that swells out of damp air and then bursts into leaves and spores. Keep the idea of waiting: the Core gives bystanders a moment to move, strike it, or step away.

A fight can be described in terms of a third element changing the outcome: fire makes a swollen, violent blast, lightning sends the seed flying at the nearest foe. Do not have characters speak of seconds, caps of five cores, or percentages. Cores harming allies is a good dramatic hazard, though a minor one.

Examples: A Hydro slime is soaked by a Hydro attack; a Dendro arrow then lands, and a glowing seed forms at its feet. Left alone it bursts in a green shower. If a spark of lightning hits it first, it darts across the field at the nearest enemy.

Because Hyperbloom can home in on an ally when an enemy or the environment sets it off, an enemy with Electro can plausibly send a seed toward the party.

Limits: Do not claim Bloom can happen without Dendro and Hydro, or that Anemo, Geo or Cryo triggers it. Do not describe Burgeon or Hyperbloom as separate elements; they are second-stage reactions of a Dendro Core.

Do not move Lunar-Bloom earlier than Version Luna I, and do not give it direct damage on its own. As of 7.1 nothing newer than Luna I is recorded here for Bloom itself.

42.content: A Dendro Core is the bud-like object created by Bloom. It lasts up to 6 seconds and bursts for Dendro area damage within 5 m if the party member who made it is still present and alive. At most 5 can exist at a time. Pyro on it causes Burgeon; Electro on it causes Hyperbloom.

43.content: Burgeon is the reaction that follows when Pyro hits a Dendro Core. It consumes the Core and deals stronger area Dendro damage within 5 m to enemies and players. It can be triggered by a different party, or by the environment, and uses the Pyro applier's stats.

44.content: Hyperbloom is the reaction that follows when Electro hits a Dendro Core. The Core becomes a Sprawling Shot that homes in on the nearest enemy (or ally, if an enemy or the environment triggered it) and deals stronger Dendro area damage in a 1 m radius.

45.content: A Bountiful Core is a Bloom variant created by certain talents and event buffs. It bursts 0.4 seconds after it appears, with a 6.5 m radius, and cannot be turned into Burgeon or Hyperbloom. Like a Dendro Core, it harms players for only 2% of its damage to enemies.

46.content:
Bond of Life (also: Life Bond): Bond of Life is a combat mechanic that prevents healing. Some enemy, weapon or talent effects place it on a character; while it lasts it soaks up incoming healing instead of restoring health. It is a gameplay abstraction, not a story concept.

It was introduced in version 4.0. In the game it appears as a red outline over the character's HP bar.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): while Bond of Life is active, healing the character is absorbed by the bond according to its value rather than restoring HP. It clears once healing equal to its value has been taken in, or when the player visits a Statue of The Seven.

- Maximum value: 200% of the character's Max HP.
- Display: the red outline covers half as much of the HP bar as its value, so a 100% bond overlays 50% of the bar.
- Timeout: if not cleared sooner, it clears 600 seconds (10 minutes) after its last increase.
- After the bond clears, some sources apply additional effects, which depend on whatever applied it.

- Sources: certain enemies, weapons, artifacts and character talents apply or interact with it, and some talents and constellations scale with its value (the wiki keeps category lists of these).
- A weapon wielder does not receive that weapon's buff if the bond is cleared by a Statue of The Seven rather than by healing.
- Interface quirk: when a character with the bond eats healing foods such as apples, sunsettia, starshroom variants or bulle fruit, the notification reads "decreased" rather than "increased".

The wiki sorts related content by category: talents and constellations that scale with the bond, talents related to it, artifacts, weapons with passives that involve it, and enemies that apply it. Exact members change between versions, so check the in-game text of a specific item before citing it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): portray it as a debt or curse on the body that makes recovery feel useless for a while, with relief at the statue. Do not quote the percentages in character or invent a lore origin for it.

Because healing goes to paying off the bond, a healer in a scene may find their power seemingly wasted on a bonded ally. Pairing this with the Statue of The Seven as the place where it lifts matches the mechanic but is an interpretation, not stated canon.

Limits: No in-world account exists; keep it to a combat effect.

Figures above are those listed on the wiki as of 7.1 and may change in later versions.

47.comment: Bond of Life: Bond of Life numbers
47.content: Bond of Life caps at 200% of Max HP, clears after healing equal to its value or after 600 seconds since its last increase, and also clears at a Statue of The Seven.

48.content:
Burgeon (also: Burgeon reaction, Pyro Bloom reaction, Pyro-Dendro Core reaction): Burgeon is a Dendro elemental reaction. A Dendro Core (the seed-like orb a Bloom leaves behind) that is struck by Pyro explodes immediately, in a bigger burst of Dendro damage than the core would deal on its own. It is one of the two ways to cash in a Bloom early, the other being Hyperbloom.

It debuted in Version 3.0 together with Bloom, Hyperbloom, Quicken, Spread and Aggravate, the reactions introduced for Dendro. The reaction cannot happen on its own: a Hydro and Dendro Bloom has to make the core first.

In universe: Canon gives no in-world explanation for Burgeon. The pages read treat it purely as a combat rule, so it is best understood as what fire does to a ripe seed of plant energy.

Gameplay: Gameplay: when Pyro is applied to a Dendro Core, Burgeon triggers. It uses up the core and deals Dendro area damage, wider and heavier than an unaided core burst.

- A Dendro Core normally explodes by itself when its time runs out, but only if the character who made it is still in the party and alive. Burgeon detonates it early, in a 5 m radius.
- The wiki says the damage hits enemies and players alike; damage to players from Bloom-related reactions is 2% of the damage to enemies.
- It can be triggered by a party other than the one that made the Bloom, including the environment, and its damage scales with the party that applied the Pyro.
- Burgeon is a transformative reaction: it does its own damage, based on the triggering character's level and Elemental Mastery, and ignores ATK and cannot critically strike unless a talent or constellation allows it.

- A target can take only two instances of damage from each Bloom-related reaction per source every 0.5 seconds, and that limit is separate for each triggering character. Dendro Core explosions and Bountiful Core explosions are counted separately.
- Burgeon cannot be triggered on Bountiful Cores, which are the quick-bursting cores some abilities and event buffs make instead of ordinary Dendro Cores. They share the limit of five cores with normal ones.
- Hyperbloom, the Electro version, sends the core as a homing Sprawling Shot instead of exploding it where it lies. At most five Dendro Cores can exist at once.

- Version 3.0 added the Dendro Elemental Resonance Sprawling Greenery, which gives nearby party members 20 Elemental Mastery for 6 seconds after Burgeon (or Spread, Aggravate, Hyperbloom), against 30 for Burning, Quicken or Bloom.
- The wiki lists talents, constellations and artifacts that raise Burgeon damage, let it critically strike or add flat damage; these are character-specific and not detailed here.
- Lunar-Bloom (the Moonsign version of the Dendro-Hydro reaction, which the wiki says replaces Bloom) also spawns a core. Treat Lunar-Bloom as a separate reaction.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show a green, lumpy seed of energy hanging in the air, then a flame touching it and the seed bursting outward in a flare of leaves, sap and heat. Keep it a sudden, loud, fairly local blast.

It reads best as a team move: one person coaxes the seed out with water and plants, another flicks fire at it. Make the Pyro user's contribution matter; the burst is theirs. Scale it to a skirmish, not a firestorm that levels a village.

Avoid having Burgeon work without a core being present, avoid claiming a Dendro-only or Pyro-only user can trigger it alone, and avoid giving it an origin story. Do not describe it as destroying forests; the effect is a short, small blast.

Limits: Burgeon needs a Dendro Core, so it needs Bloom first. It does nothing to a Bountiful Core.

The explosion can hurt the party too, though far less than it hurts enemies. The core vanishes after its duration if its creator has left the party.

Examples: Gameplay example: Hydro and Dendro together leave a Dendro Core. A Pyro attack on it triggers Burgeon at once and the core blows up in a wide Dendro burst, catching enemies close together.

49.content: A Dendro Core is what the Bloom reaction (Dendro with Hydro) leaves behind. If left alone it bursts after about six seconds. Pyro on it triggers Burgeon, Electro triggers Hyperbloom. No more than five can exist at a time.

50.content:
Burning (also: Burning reaction, Burning aura): Burning is what happens when Pyro and Dendro meet on a target, in either order. It sets the target alight: fire damage over time, a small burst of flame around them, and a flaming aura that lasts while the Dendro on the target lasts. Plants and grass catch fire the same way.

The fire consumes the Dendro as it burns, so it goes out when the plant energy is spent. The wiki lists Burning as a Transformative reaction.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Burning appears in tutorials and combat, not in character dialogue in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from.

The wiki's Environment section ties it to the open world: Wood objects such as grass, haystacks, shrubs, small trees, crates and barrels burn when Pyro touches them, and a burning creature spreads flame to combustible things it touches.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): applying Pyro to a Dendro-affected target, or Dendro to a Pyro-affected one, triggers Burning. It deals area Pyro damage and applies 1 gauge unit of Pyro within a 1 m radius to players and enemies, with a 2 second internal cooldown on that Pyro application. The Burning aura looks like an animated Pyro aura and coexists with the underlying Pyro and Dendro auras.

- The Dendro aura is steadily consumed during Burning. The state needs both the Burning aura and the Dendro aura, and ends when either runs out.
- Burning cannot damage off-field characters. Switching away pauses the damage ticks but not the Dendro consumption; if the character returns while still affected by Dendro, they resume taking damage.
- For effects that trigger on reactions, such as the Scroll of the Hero of Cinder City artifact set and Nahida's Seeds of Skandha, refreshing a Burning aura with more Pyro or Dendro does not count as triggering Burning again.

- Immunity: some enemies are immune to Burning damage, including its Poise damage and Pyro application, even when not immune to Pyro itself. The wiki lists Pyro Slimes (and Large Pyro Slimes), Pyro Specters, the Pyro Hilichurl Shooter, Hilichurl Berserker, Hilichurl Grenadier, Pyro Whopperflower, Blazing Axe Mitachurl, Pyro Abyss Mage, Abyss Lector: Fathomless Flames, the Pyro Hypostasis and the Pyro Regisvine. Every Burning-immune enemy has Pyro in some form, but not every Pyro enemy is immune; the Fatui Skirmisher - Pyroslinger Bracer is the wiki's example.
- Environment: burning grass deals damage by the grass's own level; burning bushes deal none but still apply Pyro; other burning objects deal damage using the stats of the character who set them alight. Burned grass is charred and cannot be burned again until the area resets, while shrubs and small trees are temporarily destroyed. Pyro objects such as lit bonfires and stoves can be set to Burning by applying Dendro.
- Tri-Lakshana creatures that are not enemies are Dendro objects. They react with Hydro and Electro as Bloom and Quicken, but Pyro simply strips their Dendro status without causing Burning.
- Damage is Transformative: it comes from the triggering character's level and Elemental Mastery and is resisted by the target's Pyro RES.

Talents, constellations and artifact sets exist that raise Burning damage, reduce Pyro RES against it, or let it critically strike; the wiki holds them in category tables, which this entry does not copy.

Relation to bloom: Burning is separate from Burgeon, the Pyro-on-Dendro-Core reaction in the Bloom family. Burning needs Dendro on a target; Burgeon needs a Dendro Core, which only Dendro meeting Hydro (Bloom) creates.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Burning as stubborn fire clinging to something green: leaves curling and blackening, sparks dropping from a smouldering target, grass flaring along the path of a burning enemy. It feeds on the plant energy and dies when that is gone.

Make the stakes physical and local: spreading fire in a meadow, scorched earth, an enemy who stops burning when its leafy covering is consumed. Do not have a Pyro user ignite stone, water, or a person's body without a canon reason.

Examples: An archer's Dendro arrow sticks to a hilichurl's wooden shield. A fire-slime spark touches it and flames climb the grain, spilling onto the dry grass around it.

Since a burning creature spreads fire to grass it touches, a chase through a meadow plausibly leaves a trail of ash behind it.

Limits: Burning requires both Pyro and Dendro; Anemo, Geo, Hydro, Electro and Cryo do not cause it. Do not describe it as an instant burst; its identity is the continuing burn. A burning character who is switched off the field stops taking Burning damage until they return.

Do not claim Burning affects every Pyro creature: many Pyro enemies are immune to it. Do not mix it up with Burgeon, which is a Bloom-family explosion.

51.content: The Burning aura is the flaming overlay created by the Burning reaction. It coexists with ordinary Pyro and Dendro auras and ends when either the Burning aura or the Dendro aura is used up. Refreshing it with more Pyro or Dendro does not count as another Burning reaction for reaction-triggered effects.

52.content: Some Pyro-related enemies are immune to Burning damage, its Poise damage and its Pyro application: Pyro Slimes, Pyro Specters, certain Pyro hilichurls and mitachurls, Pyro Whopperflowers, Pyro Abyss Mages, the Abyss Lector: Fathomless Flames, the Pyro Hypostasis and the Pyro Regisvine. Not every Pyro enemy shares it.

53.content:
Constellation (also: Constellations, Stella Fortuna, star sign, constellation level): "Constellation" means two linked things in Teyvat. In lore, the stars of a constellation stand for a person's fate, and the Heavenly Principles are said to pull those stars like strings on the people of the mortal world. In gameplay, each playable character has six Constellation levels, upgrades unlocked one at a time with that character's Stella Fortuna.

Every Vision holder has a personal star sign: Jean's is Leo Minor, which canon reads as strength and responsibility shouldered too young. The Traveler, Archons, adepti and a few others have special constellations that depict them personally.

In universe: The stars of Teyvat are tied to Fate. Constellations are an extension of that idea: patterns of Stella Fortuna that trace what a person will be, and strings by which the Heavenly Principles direct mortals.

Each Vision holder's fate is linked to a specific constellation, and each constellation represents particular characteristics. Jean's Leo Minor represents "strength and responsibility shouldered too young." People without Visions have fates that are also reflected in the stars, but they do not seem to be tied to named constellations. The stars themselves are physical celestial bodies called Stella Fortuna.

Dragons, which predate the Heavenly Principles' control over Teyvat, and Descenders are not subject to this puppeteering, per Neuvillette's character story and the Sovereigns' council records the wiki cites. Beings who are "overseers of the mortal realm" or who "defy the world itself" are instead given special constellations that depict them. The wiki's list of such cases includes the Traveler, the Seven Archons (Furina among them), the adepti, Albedo, Durin, Yae Miko, the Wanderer, Neuvillette, Flins, Columbina and Sandrone. Their constellation names often translate into their own titles: Venti's is Carmen Dei ("God's Song"), Zhongli's is Lapis Dei ("God's Stone"), Durin's is Draco Rubedo ("Red Dragon"), Albedo's is Princeps Cretaceus ("Chalk Prince") and the Wanderer's is Peregrinus ("Wanderer").
Such beings can still be given a constellation later: Ineffa, a part of Ix Raq'lapuj Chue'q Buluk's mind that was given its own consciousness, has one.

Some people can handle "inauspicious stars". Raiden Ei's Elemental Skill, Transcendence: Baleful Omen, refers to them, and Citlali says she can bind her own Stella Fortuna into objects. She also notes that her Stella Fortuna "return" every year on her birthday, which the wiki reads as a Vision holder's constellation being unusually reachable that day. In the limited-time event Unreconciled Stars, a constellation was shown falling as meteors; canon does not say why.
The Little Witch and the Undying Fire likens the stars to strings by which the Heavenly Principles puppeteer humans. In Competition on the Sands, Layla wonders whether Ley Lines are the reflection of the constellations seen from above, and Teleport Waypoints are said to follow "a certain order"; treat this as a hint, not a fact.

Fate and changes: The wiki's Fate page says that after Irminsul was destroyed in the Archon Quest "Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana" (6.6), the artificial system of Fate cannot be as easily directed by Celestia. It also records that Barbeloth, inspecting Durin after his fate was rewritten, found that his fate no longer existed among the stars. Do not generalise these two cases to all constellations.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): each playable character (the Traveler is handled separately) has six Constellation levels, unlocked in order by spending one Stella Fortuna per level. Constellation effects work like extra passive talents: they raise effectiveness or add capabilities to existing abilities. The third and fifth levels are normally a three-level boost to one specific Combat Talent.

Stella Fortuna comes from getting duplicates of a character from Wishes, and the 4-star kind can also come from Paimon's Bargains or events. Some 5-star characters' Stella Fortuna can be earned through the periodic event "To Temper Thyself and Journey Far". A character's Stella Fortuna cannot be used for anyone else. Once a character is at Constellation level 6, further duplicates are converted into Masterless Stella Fortuna. Talent info screens do not show the changes that Constellation effects make to talents, except the direct talent-level increases. Lyney's third level (Version 4.0) was the first to raise the Normal Attack level instead of the Skill. Aloy's Constellation levels cannot be unlocked and have no listed effects.

The Traveler has no Constellation until they align with an element. Their levels are not bought with Stella Fortuna: they come from Archon Quests, Souvenir Shops, Adventure Rank rewards (Anemo only), Statue of The Seven upgrades (Electro, Dendro, Hydro and Cryo) and Primal Flame Resonance through Tribe Reputation (Pyro only).

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): characters rarely discuss "Constellation 3" as a number; in-world, a constellation is a star sign and a hint of fate. Use it for atmosphere (a character glancing at the stars, an astrologer reading a pattern) rather than game talk. Mona is the natural voice for this, since she reads fortunes.

Keep the gameplay system out of the fiction unless the user asks about it. Keep the fate theme ambiguous: canon says the Heavenly Principles impose Fate, and that Descenders and dragons are not bound by it, but it does not say the stars dictate every choice.

54.content: Stella Fortuna are the physical stars that make up a constellation in lore. In gameplay, they are the item that unlocks one Constellation level for the matching character; extra copies at level 6 convert into Masterless Stella Fortuna.

55.content: Constellations are named in Latin-style terms that sometimes match the character: Jean's Leo Minor, Venti's Carmen Dei ("God's Song"), Zhongli's Lapis Dei ("God's Stone"), Albedo's Princeps Cretaceus ("Chalk Prince"), Durin's Draco Rubedo ("Red Dragon") and Xiao's Alatus Nemeseos ("Winged Nemesis"). Columbina is the only character whose constellation name equals her own name.

56.content:
Cryo (also: Cryo element, element of ice, element of frost): Cryo is the element of ice and frost, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is Anastasya, the Tsaritsa (divine name Vassaga), God of Love, who rules Snezhnaya, the land of eternal winter. Cryo users chill, freeze and slow their enemies. The Tsaritsa also holds the Cryo Gnosis and, as of 7.1, five of the other six.

Cryo ascension gems are Shivada Jade. The Cryo Dragon Sovereign is long dead, and its corpse is tied to Snezhnaya's ice and crystal ley lines. Cryoculi were added in Snezhnaya in Version 7.0.

In universe: Most people cannot use Cryo. Those who can usually hold a Cryo Vision, a crystal that grants control of the element. The Tsaritsa draws instead on the Cryo Authority of her divine throne in Celestia, and on her Gnosis.

Snezhnaya is the element's home in the world. In the far north is Morepesok, the only port city on the northern coast, known for its birch forests and old forestry industry. In gameplay the Cryo status can coat certain objects as well as creatures, such as ore, Thunderwood and Amber's Baron Bunny, so reactions can occur on them. Frozen is a sibling element carried by enemy ice shields and some Cryo creatures; the Frozen reaction (Cryo with Hydro) holds a target in place.

Origins: Origins, as canon tells them. Like all the elemental Authorities, Cryo first belonged to one of the Seven Sovereigns, the elemental dragons of the old world. The Heavenly Principles stole part of those powers and tied them to the Divine Thrones, which became the Archons' Authorities (revealed in the Fontaine Archon Quest, 4.1); Visions derive from them too. In the Natlan Archon Quest (5.1), the Lord of the Night says the Heavenly Principles created elemental energy by dividing the Light Realm's raw currents into seven with Phlogiston as a base. How an Archon relates to their element, and why a nation takes on its element's character, remains unexplained.

The Cryo Dragon went to war against Celestia with the other sovereigns and was defeated. According to the wiki's account of the 7.x story, the people of Hyperborea then tried to use its corpse to create a Primordial Human with an authority equal to Nibelung's. The attempt went out of control. The corpse's unchecked authority left Snezhnaya with a form of Holy Soil phenomenon, covering the land in primordial ice and turning ley lines into veins of crystal, and Hyperborea was struck by a Celestial Nail. The experiment still produced a living being: the Belyi Tsar emerged a thousand years later from the dragon's remains, which had stayed above ground with their authority suppressed by the nail. In the 7.1 Archon Quest, Ronova, her authority revoked and mortally wounded by Pierro, placed Eitr on the nail, which crumbled and left the dragon's corpse free to hallow the soil of the whole world.

Archon and nation: Archon: Anastasya Feodorovna Snezhnaya, the Tsaritsa of All Snezhnaya, Cryo Archon of the Seven and God of Love. Her divine name is Vassaga. Nation: Snezhnaya, which she governs directly from Zapolyarny Palace.

She became Cryo Archon about 500 years ago, during the Cataclysm, succeeding the Belyi Tsar after his death on an expedition. Unlike most Archons she runs her nation day to day: her Edicts are the highest authority, and the Fatui, who handle most governance, carry out her will abroad. After the Cataclysm she cut ties with the other Archons, including Venti.

Early in her reign some Snowland Fae nobles refused to accept a non-fae ruler. She stripped rebellious princes of their titles, had the Fatui build the fortress Glupov, set up the Snezhnograd Veche (headed by a human) in place of fae rule, and approved Nod-Krai's autonomy under the Lightkeepers. She appoints the Eleven Fatui Harbingers. She is not a fae despite her pointed ears. As God of Love she refuses to use that authority, saying the love the Heavenly Principles force on the gods is false and coerced.

In the 7.1 Archon Quest she is shown directly: she ends the investigation of the Traveler and explains why she wants the Gnoses. In the follow-up World Quest A Letter From Zapolyarny Palace she names the Traveler "Consultant to the Tsaritsa". Her subordinates, including Vesna and Danica, believe she is kinder than she thinks herself, while others describe her as cold and stern. Her private history belongs in her own entry.

Gnosis and authority: In Ending Note (Prologue, 1.0), Venti explained that a Gnosis is an Archon's internal focus that resonates directly with Celestia, and that the Fatui were gathering them. The Cryo Gnosis is the Tsaritsa's own; her power comes from both it and the Cryo Authority of her Divine Throne.

Besides the Cryo Gnosis, the Tsaritsa gained the Anemo and Geo Gnoses, then the Electro, Dendro and Hydro Gnoses; the Pyro Gnosis never reached her. In the teaser "A Winter Night's Lazzo", the Harbingers gather to mourn Signora while the Anemo and Geo Gnoses sit as chess pieces on Pierro's board and an unseen cold moves the opposing pieces; the mausoleum is then frozen over.

In the 7.1 Archon Quest the Gnoses are shown to be the remains of the Third Descender, Saarelainen, split into seven when the Heavenly Principles agreed to resurrect Anastasya after erasing her. Using her Cryo mastery together with six Gnoses, she created a realm of slowed time inside a room of her palace to stall Rhinedottir, so the Shade could not finish reviving Ronova's victims before Celestia's next monitoring cycle. This is the clearest canon example of Cryo reaching beyond ice into the laws of Reason. She also keeps a seal left by the Third Descender, which she believes needs all seven Gnoses to open.

Snezhnaya present: Version 7.0 added Snezhnaya as a playable region, with Cryoculi, Statues of The Seven and terrain that players can freeze, shatter and reshape. By the time the Traveler arrived in inner Snezhnaya, the Tsaritsa was away on a campaign in the east against a monster causing endless snowstorms; she ended up going alone, and returned after eliminating it. Nod-Krai (6.x) remains autonomous territory within Snezhnaya.

Elemental beings: Cryo Slimes, Specters, Cicins, Whopperflowers, Regisvines, Abyss Mages and the Cryo Hypostasis are Cryo creatures. The Cryo Dragon Sovereign is dead.

Archive entries describe Cryo Slimes as small monsters formed where Cryo coagulates in nature; in gameplay they freeze the water beneath them, so they cannot drown. Cryo Specters are floating monsters of concentrated Cryo. Cryo Regisvines are vines imbued with biting frost from the ley lines.

- Cryo Hypostasis (code name Daleth): a high-purity Cryo entity on Dragonspine, where a great Skyfrost Nail fell in a bygone era and has been pouring energy into the ley lines since.
- Cryo Abyss Mages: Abyss creatures that condense atmospheric vapour into icicles; fragile once their barrier is broken.
- Cryo Cicins: weak creatures that manipulate Cryo only slightly. Cryo Whopperflowers: ambush plants that can grow into Regisvines over years.
- A certain alchemist who studied Cryo Specters speculated they might be a kind of Slime, or like the Traveler, since none needed a Vision; his teacher reprimanded him.

Known uses: Chilling and freezing foes, raising ice, and slowing movement.

In Snezhnaya the ice can be broken, shattered and rebuilt to change terrain and enemy movement. Dragonspine's Sheer Cold is an environmental hazard of its climate, separate from the Cryo element.

- The Tsaritsa froze Signora's whole mausoleum, and in 7.1 froze a monster created by the Ruler of Life in the Northland Bank vaults before Rhinedottir stopped her.
- Skirk, who is not a Vision holder, disguises Abyssal power as Cryo with the Seven-Shifting Serpent technique learned from Surtalogi.
- Cryo Vision holders include Ganyu, Kaeya, Qiqi, Chongyun, Diona, Eula, Rosaria, Shenhe, Kamisato Ayaka, Layla, Wriothesley, Mika, Charlotte, Freminet, Citlali and Escoffier; the origin of each Vision belongs in that character's file.

Venti told the Traveler in Ending Note that Vision holders are "allogenes" who may one day ascend to godhood in Celestia. A dead holder's Vision becomes Masterless and loses its power.

Limits: Cryo does not react with Dendro.

A Vision fixes its holder to one element. Masterless Visions lose their element and power when their holder dies.

Gameplay: Cryo slimes, specters and the Cryo Hypostasis are immune to Cryo, and Cryo-shielded enemies carry the Frozen element, which does not react with Hydro. The Cryo status slows animation speed of affected targets by 15%. Cryo is not Sheer Cold: it is a status applied to characters and objects.

Interactions: Cryo reacts with Electro (Superconduct), Hydro (Frozen), Pyro (Melt), Anemo (Swirl, and Stellar Swirl since 7.0) and Geo (Crystallize). Each has its own entry.

Frozen holds a target in place, and a blunt or Geo hit shatters it. Superconduct lowers Physical resistance. Melt amplifies Cryo hits on Pyro-affected targets. Swirl spreads Cryo to nearby targets, and Crystallize leaves a Cryo shard that gives a shield.

Stellar-Conduct (Cryo with Electro) and Stellar Swirl (Cryo with Anemo) are the Stellar Glimmer versions of Superconduct and Swirl, added in 7.0; each has its own entry.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Cryo is a damage type and the element of characters such as Ganyu, Kaeya, Qiqi, Chongyun, Diona, Eula, Rosaria, Shenhe, Kamisato Ayaka, Layla, Wriothesley, Mika, Charlotte, Freminet, Citlali, Escoffier, Skirk and Aloy. The Traveler becomes Cryo by resonating with a Statue of The Seven in Snezhnaya.

The Elemental Resonance "Shattering Ice" (two or more Cryo characters) shortens the Electro status on the party by 40% and raises CRIT Rate by 15% against targets that are Frozen or affected by Cryo. Cryoculi are offered at Statues of The Seven in Snezhnaya (about 140 in the overworld; they do not respawn). Ascension gems are Shivada Jade.

Gameplay recent: Gameplay, recent additions: Stellar Swirl (Anemo with Cryo) and Stellar-Conduct (Cryo with Electro) joined the Stellar Glimmer reactions in 7.0. In Snezhnaya, Cryo can break, shatter and reshape terrain. The Elements page lists some Snezhnayan characters' element source as a Stellar Linchpin rather than a Vision.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Cryo as stillness, pale blue-white light and falling temperature: breath fogging, frost creeping from a hand, ice that rings or cracks. Keep scale proportionate: a Vision holder can chill a drink, freeze a puddle or raise an ice barrier, but sealing a whole mausoleum in ice is the Archon's work.

Cryo can preserve and restrain as well as hurt: frosted windows, a cooled cellar, a held breath. A Snezhnayan can speak of the cold as ordinary rather than hostile. The Tsaritsa rules in person, so she is a visible head of state, not a distant myth.

Do not give every Cryo user control over time. Do not have a Cryo Vision holder know the story of the Cryo Dragon, Saarelainen or the Gnoses unless the scene establishes how they learned it. As of 7.1 the Cryo Gnosis and five others are with the Tsaritsa; the Pyro Gnosis is not.

57.content:
The Cryo Archon is Anastasya Feodorovna Snezhnaya, the Tsaritsa of All Snezhnaya, called the God of Love among the Seven. Her divine name is Vassaga. She succeeded the Belyi Tsar about 500 years ago, rules Snezhnaya from Zapolyarny Palace and appoints the Eleven Fatui Harbingers. She holds the Cryo Gnosis and refuses to use her authority of love.

As of 7.1 she holds six Gnoses (all but Pyro), and in a 7.1 World Quest she appoints the Traveler "Consultant to the Tsaritsa". Her own entry carries her biography and relationships.

58.content:
The Cryo Dragon was one of the Seven Sovereigns, the dragon-lords who ruled Teyvat before the Heavenly Principles. It fought Celestia and was defeated. Its corpse is the source of Snezhnaya's primordial ice and crystal ley lines.

Hyperborea used the corpse in an attempt to make a Primordial Human, and the Belyi Tsar emerged from its remains a thousand years later. A Celestial Nail suppressed its authority until it crumbled in the 7.1 Archon Quest, freeing the corpse to hallow the soil of the world.

59.content: Cryoculi are found scattered across Snezhnaya and are offered at Statues of The Seven there. Item text calls the Cryoculus a substance "that has accumulated intense Cryo energy", offered to help a Statue regain power lost over the years. They appeared in 7.0.

60.content: Cryo Slimes form where Cryo coagulates in nature and, in gameplay, freeze the water under them so they cannot drown. Cryo Specters are floating monsters of concentrated Cryo that, in gameplay, grow bigger and gain enhanced attacks after taking heavy hits. The Cryo Hypostasis (code name Daleth) is a high-purity Cryo boss on Dragonspine, where a fallen Skyfrost Nail feeds the ley lines. Cryo Regisvines are monstrous vines that absorbed frost from the ley lines and may grow from Cryo Whopperflowers. Cryo Abyss Mages call on Cryo in battle, and Cryo Cicins manipulate it only slightly. In gameplay these creatures are immune to Cryo.

61.content:
Crystallize (also: Crystallize reaction, Crystallize shard, Crystallize shield, Elemental Shard): Crystallize is what happens when Geo hits a target already affected by Pyro, Hydro, Electro or Cryo. It deals no damage. It leaves a shard of that element, and a character who picks the shard up gains a shield of the same element.

Geo is always the second element in this reaction. Anemo and Dendro are not part of it.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Crystallize shows up in tutorials and combat, not in character dialogue in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from.

The in-game tutorial describes it simply: Geo contacting Hydro, Pyro, Cryo or Electro creates shards of the matching element that give the character an elemental shield, and good use of it cuts damage taken in battle.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): the shard (Electro, Pyro, Hydro or Cryo) lasts 15 seconds on the field, with a short delay before it can be picked up. Picking it up grants an elemental shield that also lasts 15 seconds. Enemies cannot pick shards up.

- If more than 3 shards are on the field, after about 2 seconds only the 3 newest remain.
- Only one Crystallize shield is active at a time; a new shard's shield overwrites the old one.
- Crystallize can trigger only once per second on the same target.
- A Geo shard from Geovishap Hatchlings or the Pure Geo Hypostasis is a different thing; its shield can coexist with a Crystallize shield instead of replacing it.

- Shield health: base health comes from the Geo user's level and is raised by a percentage based on the user's Elemental Mastery. The wiki lists base shield HP of about 91 at level 1, about 1,851 at level 90 and about 2,199 at level 100. The Mastery bonus follows 4.44 x EM / (EM + 1400), so 100 EM gives about 29.6% and 1000 EM about 185%.
- Elemental shields are 250% effective against their own element, taking only 40% as much damage from it, and raise Interruption Resistance while active.
- A Crystallize shield can coexist with other shields, but each takes full damage at once. According to the wiki's community sources, a character's Shield Strength reduces damage taken by the shields they have rather than raising the HP of shields they make.

Geo cannot be the first element on a target, so Crystallize is always Geo applied second. Several characters, weapons and artifact sets interact with Crystallize shards or shields; the wiki handles those separately and this entry does not copy them.

Lunar crystallize: Lunar-Crystallize (own entry) is the Moonsign form of Geo meeting Hydro, which the wiki records as introduced in Version Luna IV. It needs a party member with a qualifying Moonsign Benediction passive. According to the wiki, triggering it creates three Moondrifts around the target; every third Lunar-Crystallize reaction makes them resonate in Moondrift Harmony, a tracking projectile that deals Geo damage. Moondrifts count as Geo constructs.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Crystallize as a coloured stone shard forming in the air around a struck foe: ember-red from fire, blue from water, pale from frost, violet from lightning. Picking it up wraps the character in a pane of matching light.

It is a defensive reaction, so it suits support and tank characters: a Geo user turning the enemy's own element into protection. Keep the shard visible and brief, so there is a moment to pick it up. Do not have characters count shield HP or seconds.

Examples: A Pyro slime is scorched by a sword, then struck by a Geo strike. A red crystal flies loose, and the character who gathers it is wrapped in a shell of fire-coloured light, which takes less harm from flames.

A Geo user fighting an Electro-soaked foe can make violet shards, while a Hydro foe produces blue ones. They disappear if not collected.

Limits: Crystallize does not deal damage and does not work with Dendro or Anemo. Enemies cannot pick up the shards.

Do not call Crystallize shields permanent or stackable; one at a time, and the 15-second duration is the limit. Do not move Lunar-Crystallize earlier than Version Luna IV. As of 7.1, the wiki records only the 1.0 introduction for base Crystallize.

62.content: A Crystallize shard is the pick-up created by the reaction: Electro, Pyro, Hydro or Cryo according to the element that was crystallised. It can be collected after a short delay and lasts 15 seconds on the field. Only the three newest shards stay if more are produced, and enemies cannot take them.

63.content: The shield granted by a Crystallize shard matches the shard's element and lasts 15 seconds. Its health is based on the Geo user's level and Elemental Mastery. It blocks 2.5 times as much damage from its own element, and only one such shield is active at a time.

64.content:
Delusion (also: Delusions, Evil Eye, Fatui Delusion, counterfeit Vision): Delusions are Vision-like devices made by the Fatui. They let their wielders command an element, can be used by almost anyone, and are said to be far stronger than Visions. The price is the user's vitality: they can drain life force, age the wearer or backfire fatally. How they are made is secret; the evidence points to the remains of dead gods. The Chinese name means "Evil Eye", a counterpart to the "Eye of God".

Few Fatui members outside the Eleven Harbingers hold one, and the Tsaritsa grants them herself, according to the Fatui member Viktor. In practice, Delusions have also been handed to ordinary people in Inazuma and carried by defectors abroad. As of 7.1 the Fatui are working on a finished model that drains only the regenerable part of a user's life force.

In universe: A Delusion looks like a Vision with a Fatui emblem instead of an element symbol. It is a glass orb in a jagged frame, and its colour follows the element it grants. Unlike a Vision, which the gods give to one person, a Delusion can be used by anyone who holds it.

Viktor calls Delusions the pride of the Fatui and says they come by the Tsaritsa's own hand. Pyro Agents, Cicin Mages, Mirror Maidens, Operatives and Oprichniki soldiers are all seen with Delusions in the colour of their element. The Fatui treat the subject as a closely guarded secret, even among themselves.

- In hindsight, players first see one at work in the Prologue, when Signora's blizzard freezes Venti's legs: the power is later shown to come from a Cryo Delusion given to her to suppress her fire, not boost it.
- Tartaglia's Electro Delusion was pinned on him by Pierro, called the Jester, when he became a Harbinger. He keeps a Hydro Vision as well, so a Delusion is not bound to its wearer's Vision element.
- Higher-ranking Oprichniki soldiers in Nod-Krai carry Delusions with axe-head prongs on each side.

Delusions also show up outside the Fatui's ranks. Yelena, a renegade Fatuus, kept hers when she and her brother Kirya fled to Sumeru and then Fontaine; Kirya later took it up after her death. Diluc once carried the Delusion that backfired on his father Crepus. These cases are in the entries below.

Origins and production: Canon does not describe a general method. The Delusions made in Inazuma used Crystal Marrow, which holds the Tatarigami curse of the slain god Orobashi. The wiki therefore reads Delusions as made from the remains of gods or other powerful beings, but that inference is not stated as a rule.

At the Delusion Factory on Yashiori Island (Archon Quest Chapter II, 2.1), the Traveler found rooms full of Crystal Marrow supplied by the Kanjou Commission under the Sakoku Decree. The Fatui Balladeer said openly that the Vision Hunt Decree suited the Fatui because conflict created a market for Delusions; the factory was later raided and destroyed by the Resistance.

In the manga, Delusion research is linked to experiments on injecting "archon residue" (remains of ancient gods; a translation note on the wiki says the original term means pre-Seven demon gods) into people such as Collei, and to Dottore's subordinates. That material is manga-only and is treated as uncertain.

Side effects: Delusions drain the user's life force and can backfire. Resistance soldiers in Inazuma aged rapidly; Teppei died of it. Diluc's father Crepus was fatally hurt when one backfired.

Effects vary. In the manga, Diluc carried his father's Delusion for three years without obvious ill effect, and people who already hold a Vision or wield elemental power resist abnormal elemental energy better, according to Emilie. Yelena aged quickly as she used hers to grow the Auguste flowers, and her brother Kirya, using it for the same purpose, aged himself by decades. In the manga, Delusions give off a smell of Mist Grass when used.

- Pierro's use of the Eye of the Fatui in 7.1 cost his mind and soul heavily, per Dainsleif afterwards.
- Signora's Delusion is described as different: item text frames it as the Tsaritsa's grace, offered to put out the flame that consumed her, and the wiki reports it suppressed her memories.
- Tartaglia shows a drawback only when his Delusion is combined with the Abyss technique Foul Legacy Transformation.
- Arlecchino says the drain of life force in exchange for power falls under the authority of Death (7.1).

The Jester says the Fatui's Delusions have always been an unfinished product that drains the user's life force (7.1). They are issued only on a voluntary basis: members apply for them for important missions or emergencies, and nobody is forced to take one.

Notable users: Harbingers with Delusions in canon: Tartaglia (Electro), Signora (Cryo), Arlecchino (Pyro, used when she draws on her Balemoon Bloodfire) and Pierro (Electro). Others: Fatui Agents, Cicin Mages, Mirror Maidens, Operatives and Oprichniki. Outside the Fatui: Crepus (dead), Diluc (formerly), Yelena (dead), Kirya, and Inazuma's Watatsumi Army soldiers (formerly), among them Teppei (dead).

Arlecchino wears a Pyro Vision on her back and swaps it for a Pyro Delusion when she calls on her bloodfire. Pierro hides his Electro Delusion under his clothes rather than wearing it openly.

Delusion project: In the 7.1 Archon Quest (Chapter VII Act IV, "A Rekviem for the Underworld"), the Fatui build a new model of Delusion in the Armory Palace before facing Ronova, the Ruler of Death. The Jester (Pierro) directs the project and Arlecchino volunteers as test subject, because as a descendant of the Crimson Moon she holds a share of the authority of Death, which the drain of life force falls under. Her price for taking part is that the House of the Hearth becomes independent of the Fatui and stops training children as spies. Researchers promise the new model will only draw on the regenerable part of life force. In the Traveler-assisted tests, Arlecchino's baseline power came out about three times higher than expected, but at maximum output her readings went out of control; the researchers concluded the new model had drawn on another Crimson Moon authority besides Death, an unstable variable that can induce hallucinations and loss of control. The Traveler purified the Abyssal energy in time and the test was stopped with no lasting harm to her. She judged the output still too timid to stand against Ronova.

Pierro then completed the Delusion as the "Eye of the Fatui", a more jagged form resembling the symbol of Khaenri'ah. He used it in the battle with Ronova, summoning an elemental nail whose strike, with Dainsleif and the Traveler, decided the fight. The cutscene text says it cost him his own soul and life force. Dainsleif later says the battle took an exceptionally heavy toll on his mind and soul, and Paimon notes he had not been seen all day. Ronova's authority was reclaimed by Celestia, and her Curse of Death lifted with it.

Gameplay: Gameplay, not lore: Fatui enemies carry Delusions as part of their models. Operative's Constancy, an enhancement material, is dropped by Wind and Frost Operatives and is the item tied to Delusions. In the 7.1 quest, Arlecchino is a temporary trial character who gains Bond of Life quickly during tests, and the player must keep an Abyssal Influence Index from rising too high.

Tartaglia's boss fight in the Golden House has phases where his Delusion is shown (Electro) and a final phase where Vision and Delusion swap places.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat a Delusion as a bargain, not a free power. Show the cost in the user: breathlessness, greying, a look of being older than their years. A Fatui who speaks of one should do so with pride or guarded caution, and never explain how it is made. Let someone who knows Visions sense that a Delusion feels wrong: cold, hungry and without the warm sense of being chosen.

A Fatui character will not volunteer how few people hold a Delusion; Viktor is an example of a lower-ranked member who enjoys boasting about them. In Inazuma, once soldiers began to age, Kokomi ordered the whole army to stop using Delusions and had the affected soldiers treated.

Do not claim Delusions are made of a particular god in a general way, give every Fatui a Delusion, or make the drain painless for ordinary people. Do not treat the Eye of the Fatui as standard issue; it is Pierro's.

65.content: Diluc's father Crepus used a Delusion to defeat a monster, Ursa the Drake, and it backfired and left him fatally hurt. Diluc's and Kaeya's character stories tell the outcome differently: Diluc's says Crepus died in his arms, Kaeya's says Diluc ended his father's agony. Diluc left the Knights and traced the "counterfeit Visions" to the Fatui; in the manga he also takes up his father's Delusion. In the manga it is a red orb on a glove that raises barbed chains, sometimes wrapped in black fire; this version is manga-only.

66.content: A hidden facility on Yashiori Island, found by the Traveler during the Inazuma Archon Quest (2.1). Fatui staff made Delusions there from Crystal Marrow, supplied via the Kanjou Commission. The Balladeer said the Fatui gained from the Vision Hunt Decree because it created demand. The Resistance destroyed the factory. Kokomi had already ordered the army to stop using Delusions after soldiers began to age.

67.content: Pierro's upgraded Electro Delusion, completed through the 7.1 Delusion project in time for the battle against Ronova. Its casing is jagged, with extra protrusions, and resembles the symbol of Khaenri'ah. In that fight it let Pierro summon an enormous elemental nail, powered by a surge of Abyssal energy and his own life force, and it left him drained in mind and soul. The Chinese wording for "Vision" is "Eye of God", which gives the name its sense.

68.content: Resistance soldiers, ambitious people opposed to the Vision Hunt Decree, secretly used Fatui Delusions and began to age fast. Gorou seized one, a black orb with a pale grey Fatui emblem, and showed it to the Traveler. Teppei, a soldier who never owned a Vision, had used one and was dying of its effects. Kokomi ordered the army to stop using them.

69.content: Yelena, a defected Fatui member, used her Delusion to grow Auguste flowers in Fontaine for the perfume; it aged her fast. After her death, her brother Kirya took up the Delusion to continue and to take revenge on her associates. In the 4.8 story quest "Base Note: Auguste", Emilie and Collei work out that the flowers and seeds carry elemental energy from the Delusion, which may harm sensitive people, and that using one costs the time the user has left.

70.content:
Dendro (also: Dendro element, element of plants, element of grass): Dendro is the element of plants and growth, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is the God of Wisdom, whose divine name is Buer and who today is Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida); her nation is Sumeru, a land of rainforest and desert. Dendro Visions let their holders call up vines, leaves and seeds, and it is the element behind Quicken and Bloom reactions. The Dendro Dragon Sovereign is Apep, who once ruled all of Sumeru. Nahida traded her Dendro Gnosis to the Harbinger Dottore in Chapter III, and as of 7.1 the Tsaritsa holds six Gnoses.

Dendro ascension gems are Nagadus Emeralds. Dendro was the last element to gain a playable character, arriving only in Version 3.0 with Tighnari and Collei and the Dendro-aligned Traveler. The Traveler's resonance with Dendro is remarked on by several characters in Chapter III.

In universe: Most people can only use Dendro through a Dendro Vision; Nahida draws on the Dendro Authority of her divine throne in Celestia. In Sumeru, Dendro is bound up with life, growth and dreams: the rainforest, its Aranara, and the Akasha network all trace back to the God of Wisdom.

Greater Lord Rukkhadevata, the first Dendro Archon, is credited with reviving the rainforest from desert, creating the Aranara, and guiding the people who founded the Sumeru Akademiya. Dendro is also the element of her "wisdom": the Akasha System she created used the Dendro Gnosis to link minds. Nahida, her successor, is hardly a fighter; her power is chiefly over dreams, consciousness and plants.

Dendro and "growth" are linked in a notable way. Rukkhadevata shrank to a more child-like form each time she poured her divine strength into the land, once to suppress forbidden knowledge among King Deshret's people and again during the cataclysm. Kusanali says she too could release power beyond her limits by de-aging herself, possibly down to the "blade of grass or a twig" she began as. Canon does not say whether this is true of every Dendro Archon.

Sumeru's two halves reflect the Dendro-versus-desert story. After the war of funerary flame, a Celestial Nail from the Heavenly Principles turned most of verdant Sumeru into the Great Red Sand and forced the Dendro Dragon to adapt to the dunes; the forest survived only where Rukkhadevata and her followers revived and defended it, with the Wall of Samiel marking the line. Most Sumeru residents now associate Dendro with the rainforest and the god in the Divine Tree, but ancient desert kingdoms such as King Deshret's also lived under her protection.

Origins: Origins, as canon tells them. The elemental Authorities first belonged to the Seven Sovereigns, the elemental dragons of the old world. The Heavenly Principles stole part of that power and tied it to the Divine Thrones, which became the Archons' Authorities (revealed in the Fontaine Archon Quest, 4.1); Visions also derive from these Authorities. The Natlan Archon Quest (5.1) reveals that the Heavenly Principles made elemental energy by dividing the raw elemental currents of the Light Realm into seven, using Phlogiston as a base. Why an Archon is tied to their element, and why a nation takes on its element's character, remains unexplained; Sumeru is the former domain of the Dendro Dragon Sovereign Apep.

Archon and nation: Archon: the God of Wisdom, divine name Buer. The current holder is Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida); before her it was Greater Lord Rukkhadevata. Nation: Sumeru, whose capital Sumeru City is built on the Divine Tree.

Rukkhadevata perished in the cataclysm about 500 years ago. Before dying she created Kusanali as her next incarnation, but she had exhausted herself fighting the Abyss, so Kusanali was born as a child with no memories. In Chapter III's finale (Where the Boat of Consciousness Lies), Nahida removed all memory of Rukkhadevata from Irminsul at Rukkhadevata's own request, to eradicate forbidden knowledge from the world. As a result everyone, Nahida included, now believes Kusanali has always been the sole Dendro Archon; only the Traveler remembers the truth.

The Sumeru Akademiya's sages shut the young god in the Sanctuary of Surasthana for centuries, disappointed that she lacked her predecessor's wisdom, and ran Sumeru through the Akasha System instead. Before the 2.1 update, Chinese text never gave the Dendro Archon pronouns, which led some localisations to call the God of Wisdom male; 2.1 confirmed Kusanali as female and corrected the English text.

Canon also records an older sovereignty over the same land: the Dendro Dragon Sovereign Apep ruled all Sumeru before the Heavenly Principles arrived, and nurtured the first elemental lifeforms. In the sands, Rukkhadevata once co-reigned with Nabu Malikata and King Deshret as the "Three Eternal Companion-Gods", before breaking with them when they planned to turn against Celestia; she then founded her own domain by nurturing a rainforest.

Gnosis and authority: Dendro's Gnosis belonged first to Rukkhadevata and powered the Akasha System, then to Nahida. In Chapter III Nahida gave Dottore the Dendro Gnosis in exchange for knowledge about the false sky. She also took the Electro Gnosis from Scaramouche's fallen "Shouki no Kami" and later gave it to Dottore in exchange for his agreeing to erase his Segments. A Gnosis is not required for an Archon to hold their power: Nahida stays the Dendro Archon with no Dendro Gnosis.

The Gnosis connects its bearer directly to Celestia. Nahida needed an additional Gnosis (the Electro one) to enter Rukkhadevata's realm of consciousness, and later used the Pyro Gnosis, brought by the Traveler from Mavuika, to burn the corrupted Irminsul. Dottore remarked that she could not use the Electro Gnosis in battle, so usage of another element's Gnosis may be restricted.

Gnosis count as of 7.1: Anastasya has collected six Gnoses (all but the Pyro Gnosis, which vanished in the aftermath of the Irminsul fire). In the 7.1 Archon Quest "A Rekviem for the Underworld" she used her Cryo mastery and the six Gnoses together to slow time in a room of her palace and stall Rhinedottir.

Gnosis event note: In the Version 6.6 Archon Quest act "Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana", Nahida and her allies, with Mavuika's Pyro Gnosis carried by the Traveler, overloaded Irminsul using the Akasha System and then burned it. Dottore, who had attacked Irminsul from within, died in the fire. The Akasha System that Rukkhadevata had made to fight forbidden knowledge was used one last time in the plan.

Elemental beings: Apep, the Dendro Dragon Sovereign, and Dendro elemental lifeforms such as slimes, specters and the Dendro Hypostasis.

Apep survived the old world's wars and is still alive; the Traveler and Nahida helped her in the 3.6 quest Homecoming. Dendro Samachurls are hilichurl shamans who attack with vines and poison; Dendro Slimes are slimes shaped by abundant Dendro in their environment, which also gives them Dendro's weaknesses.

- Apep contains an entire world inside her, the Heart of Oasis, in which she bore the first elemental lifeforms. Her attempt to gather forbidden knowledge to fight the Heavenly Principles contaminated both her and the Heart, and her creatures took on corrupted forms; Tumors of the Withering are what they become at the end of their lives. After Nahida erased forbidden knowledge, the creatures lost memories and helped restore the Heart, and Apep chose to rest and watch rather than pursue revenge.
- Dendro Specters have appeared since Version 3.0. One archive note records a researcher's conclusion that the Aranara are Dendro Specters, which quest text does not confirm.
- The Dendro Hypostasis is a boss that shoots Dendro orbs and transforms into a whip.

- The Aranara are small plant-like beings who can shape dreams. Rukkhadevata made them, and in the cataclysm they preserved the forest with the help of the Traveler's sibling.
- Dendroculi are consolidated Dendro energy; offered to Sumeru's Statues of The Seven they restore power the Statue lost over the years.

Known uses: Vines, leaves, seeds and plants grown or controlled, and Dendro Cores from Bloom. Some Dendro enemies, such as Large Dendro Slimes, inflict a poison status.

Nahida's power over dreams and consciousness is part of her Dendro Authority. Tighnari and Collei, Sumeru's rainforest rangers, hold Dendro Visions. The Sumeru rainforest itself is Rukkhadevata's work.

- The Akasha System: Rukkhadevata's design to link minds, powered by the Dendro Gnosis; the sages later repurposed it into a knowledge network accessed through Akasha Terminals.
- Dreams: Nahida can enter, shape and send dreams as part of the Dendro Authority, and Sabzeruz Festival dream loops were abused by the sages.
- Purging: when Nahida erased forbidden knowledge from Irminsul, it was also purged from Apep and her Oasis.

- Visions are personal: Tighnari's Vision fell from his clothes after a conference in which he corrected a speaker. Collei's Vision appeared in her hand after a night on a cliff beside a sleeping girl, when Tighnari feared she had used power she should not.
- The Traveler: Dendro is likely the fourth element the Traveler resonated with, and its use is remarked on in Chapter III. Later canon has the Traveler wielding all seven elements.

Limits: Dendro does not react with Anemo or Geo.

Dendro reacts with Hydro, Electro and Pyro only. A Vision fixes its bearer to one element.

Gameplay: "Wood" objects (vines, bushes, shields) behave like a lesser sibling element that can burn but cannot trigger Quicken or Bloom. Dendro Slimes, Hypostases and elemental enemies are immune to Dendro.

Interactions: Quicken (Dendro + Electro) leads to Aggravate and Spread. Bloom (Dendro + Hydro) creates a Dendro Core, which can become Hyperbloom with Electro or Burgeon with Pyro. Burning (Dendro + Pyro) ignites. Each is its own entry.

Lunar-Bloom (6.0) is a Lunar reaction version of Bloom: with certain characters in the party, Bloom becomes Lunar-Bloom and grants the party Verdant Dew.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Dendro is a damage type and the element of Nahida, Tighnari, Collei, Baizhu, Alhaitham, Kaveh, Yaoyao, Kirara, Emilie, Lauma, Nefer and others. The Traveler can switch to Dendro after resonating with a Statue of The Seven in Sumeru.

The Elemental Resonance "Sprawling Greenery" (two or more Dendro characters) raises Elemental Mastery and gives additional Elemental Mastery after Burning, Quicken, Bloom, Aggravate, Spread, Hyperbloom and Burgeon reactions. Dendroculi raise the Statues of The Seven in Sumeru (271 in the overworld), and Dendro Sigils are the currency for the Tree of Dreams' Vanarana's Favor.

Gameplay recent: Gameplay, recent additions: Lunar-Bloom (6.0, Luna I) arrived with Lauma, and Nefer (6.1, Luna II) is another Dendro character who enables it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Dendro as growth, scent and gentle light: leaves unfurling, vines tightening, fresh-cut grass, green glow with golden accents. Keep scale proportionate: a Vision holder can summon vines and seeds, not raise a forest. Dream-shaping and consciousness are Nahida's Authority, not general Dendro skills.

Narratively, Dendro grows things, including knowledge and memory: leaves, ideas, seeds, dreams. A Bloom should visibly sprout something, and Burning should show the plant catching fire. Sumeru characters often treat plants and learning as sacred.

Avoid ascribing sleep control or mind reading to any Vision holder. Do not state that Rukkhadevata exists in anyone's memory except the Traveler's. Do not give the Dendro Gnosis back to Nahida; as of 7.1 it is in the Tsaritsa's hands.

71.content:
The Dendro Archon is the God of Wisdom, protector of Sumeru. There have been two holders: Greater Lord Rukkhadevata, who died in the cataclysm about 500 years ago, and her reincarnation Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida). In Chapter III Nahida erased Rukkhadevata from Irminsul, so the world remembers only Kusanali.

Rukkhadevata created the Aranara, revived the rainforest and made the Akasha System. Kusanali was born a child with no memories because her predecessor overexerted herself fighting the Abyss.

72.content: Apep is the Dendro Dragon Sovereign. She ruled all Sumeru and created the first elemental lifeforms in an inner world, the Heart of Oasis. Attempting to gather forbidden knowledge to resist the Heavenly Principles corrupted her and her creatures. The Celestial Nail that turned Sumeru to desert forced her to adapt. After Nahida purged forbidden knowledge, the Traveler and Nahida helped restore the Heart (3.6, Homecoming), and Apep chose to rest and observe humanity and the gods.

73.content: A Dendroculus is an Adventure Item scattered across Sumeru; item text calls it a substance "that has accumulated intense Dendro energy" which can be offered to a Statue of The Seven to restore power it has lost.

74.content: Dendro Slimes have changed through ecological adaptation to abundant Dendro and burn intensely in bright flame. Dendro Samachurls are hilichurl shamans whose archive note says such shamans often peak in old age, and describes a grudge beneath the mask and poison ivy sprouting from hateful whispers. Dendro Specters have appeared since Version 3.0. The Dendro Hypostasis is a boss that shoots Dendro orbs and whips. In gameplay these are immune to Dendro (Samachurls resist it).

75.content: Nagadus Emeralds are the ascension gems used for Dendro characters.

76.content:
Diving (also: underwater exploration, Transoceanic Sourcewater, Fontaine's Blessing, Aquatic Stamina): Diving is how the Traveler explores underwater in Fontaine. Fontaine's lakes can be dived in once the first Statue of The Seven there is activated; a power called the Transoceanic Sourcewater keeps Vision holders, the Traveler and Paimon from drowning and lets them breathe and speak underwater. Ordinary people without Visions need diving gear and training. Fontaine is the only nation where diving is a game mechanic.

Diving is a recognised profession in Fontaine, and a diving certificate can be earned there, according to Vasco. It arrived in Version 4.0 with Fontaine.

In universe: The tutorial calls the power the "Transoceanic Sourcewater" and says it flows out from a Statue of The Seven to bless those moving through Fontaine's lakes. In the text of the world, it lets Vision holders (and certain others, such as the Traveler and Paimon) breathe and speak underwater.

People without Visions rely on diving gear and must complete specialised training. The diver Archenoul, hired by Spina di Rosula, says such newcomers must first go down with a professional, and warns that cramps or ringing in the ears can follow if a diver skips a warm-up or fails to adapt to water pressure. The Traveler also dives comfortably in the Sea of Bygone Eras, said to lie beneath depths untouched by sunlight, so cold and darkness do not seem to trouble them either.

Fontainians often call the great lake that lies on top of their land a "sea", although geographically it is a lake, so "underwater" in Fontaine usually means the lakes of the raised mainland. The Sea of Bygone Eras, the waters south of that lake, once belonged to the same high sea and holds the ruins of Remuria; a commission such as Days Beneath the Waves shows divers doing ordinary salvage work.

Canon does not say what the Sourcewater is. It is presented as a blessing carried by the statues, and nothing read here ties it to the Hydro Archon or to Pneuma and Ousia. Keep it a mystery rather than assigning it a source.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Diving unlocks after activating the first Statue of The Seven in Fontaine, once the quest The Outlander Who Caught the Wind is complete. While diving the party cannot drown and uses Aquatic Stamina for fast swimming instead of ordinary Stamina; Aquatic Stamina cannot be increased or unlocked further. Characters share the same underwater abilities and can still be switched. Diving works in the lakes of the raised mainland and the Sea of Bygone Eras, but not in the lower surrounding waters or around the Nostoi region (the sea around Petrichor, per the Fontaine page).

Normal Attacks, Elemental Skills and Bursts are replaced underwater. A water string stands in for the Normal Attack, and borrowed Xenochromatic Creature abilities stand in for the Skill; their damage is the same for every character regardless of level, equipment or stats. Xenochromatic Creatures are Fontemer Aberrants that never attack and cannot be harmed; striking one lets the party borrow an ability (for example the Armored Crab's shield and shockwave, or the Hunter's Ray's water blades) that lasts until the party fully leaves the water. Recovery Orbs found near schools of fish restore Aquatic Stamina and half of each character's maximum HP for the whole party. Underwater currents carry the party along set paths, and Echoing Conches or Sonar Waves reveal hidden objects. In Co-Op each ability applies only to the player who got it.

- Fontaine's Blessing is the in-game tutorial name for the Diving ability; the second tutorial explains how Sourcewater clusters beside the character let the player unleash borrowed powers.
- Characters with an Arkhe alignment show a matching aura around the Sourcewater bubble beside the active character's shoulder.
- Furina's utility passive, The Sea Is My Stage, reduces the cooldown of Xenochromatic abilities by 30%; it is the only character Talent that affects them.
- Fontemer Aberrants and specialised Clockwork Meka are met underwater, and passive Talents whose conditions can be met while diving still trigger.
- Exiting the water by sprinting makes Fontainian characters and the Traveler leap out; other characters surface slowly into ordinary Swimming.

Limits: Diving is a Fontaine mechanic and does not apply in other nations.

Ordinary Swimming outside Fontaine uses Stamina, and the party cannot fight while swimming. Non-Vision holders in the story cannot dive freely without gear and training.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the Sourcewater as a quiet, protective blessing. Vision holders, the Traveler and Paimon can talk and breathe underwater as if in air, while ordinary NPCs wear divesuits and take pre-dive precautions. Do not let an ordinary Fontainian simply dive without gear.

Underwater scenes suit slow, bright, wondering description: light fading with depth, schools of fish, currents. Keep Xenochromatic creatures non-hostile, since they never attack. Do not name the Sourcewater's origin.

77.content: The Transoceanic Sourcewater is the power behind diving in Fontaine. Tutorial text says it flows from a Statue of The Seven, protects those moving through the lakes and lets them breathe and speak underwater if they hold a Vision (and for the Traveler and Paimon). Its origin is not explained.

78.content: Xenochromatic Creatures are special Fontemer Aberrants met underwater. They do not attack and cannot be damaged, but striking one lets a diver borrow its ability, such as a shield, water blades or a thrown hat-shaped bomb, until they leave the water.

79.content: Archenoul is a diver in Poisson, Fontaine, employed by Spina di Rosula, who says they seldom take outside commissions. They explain that people without Visions need specialised training and a professional's company on first dives, and warn about cramps and pressure-related symptoms.

80.content:
Eitr (also: Embryonic-Ichoric-Telluric-Rudiment, the Eitr): The Eitr, full name Embryonic-Ichoric-Telluric-Rudiment, is a forbidden creation of Hyperborea, the lost golden city of Snezhnaya. It contains the power of the Light Realm and can be used to alter living bodies. In 7.1 the dying Ronova fused an orb of it to Snezhnaya's Celestial Nail.

The Belyi Tsar found it in the Shadow Realm, and the Hvergelmir institute later experimented with it, most visibly on a Snegovik.

In universe: Canon describes the Eitr as the final result of forbidden technology that let Hyperborea's master crafters modify the very essence of life. It carries Light Realm power. Used on a body, it can give a creature power beyond what its kind normally has.

According to the Eye of Graeae, the Belyi Tsar obtained the Eitr not long after delving into the Shadow Realm, but began Eitr research only some time afterwards; no one knows why. A note left by a noble figure at the Pale Crown Palace records that during his 446th foray into the Shadow Realm the writer found the Eitr together with records about it. Those records concern Hyperborea's fate and its attempt to reach the original light of the world.

Eitr alteration is said to leave a result similar to the makeup of the Belyi Tsar himself. The Eitr eventually came into the hands of Hvergelmir, the research institute of old Snezhnaya, where Koshchei and Pavlina experimented with it. Pavlina, princess of the Snegurochka, is said to have used Hvergelmir's techniques to modify Snegovik, giving their bodies power beyond their race's due.
