Souls can also be split, marked, shared or stored: Zibai's soul was divided into fragments, Columbina left a piece of hers in a Luonnotar, Mitya's soul bears Ronova's mark, and Moon Wheels are said to be formed of soul-stuff. The Snegovik, Snezhnaya's fae, are said to be born with incomplete souls.

These are separate local accounts, not one system. Treat any soul rule as belonging to its region and source.

In universe: - Ley Lines: the standard destination. Ronova says that after the body dies the soul must return to the Ley Lines for death to be complete.
- Night Kingdom: in Natlan the dead go there; souls become Nightsouls and eventually merge into a sea of souls.
- Ghosts: souls or echoes that did not make the transition and linger on the surface.

- Irminsul: a record of everything in Teyvat; Nahida says the one way to enter it that she could not guard was through death.
- The moons: in an older age, boatmen ferried the noble dead to cities on the moons.

Ronova claims that death gives mortals wisdom: souls connect to all things and see the chain of cause and effect. Mortals experiencing the afterlife in the Korolevskiy Theater looked and felt physical, which Odette noted as odd for something non-physical; Mitya concluded their bodies there were shells in the afterlife.

Ley lines and death: In the Wraith's Nocturne quest (7.0), Ronova explains that after the physical body dies, the soul must return to the Ley Lines for that person's death to be considered complete, and that her Authority covers the whole process, including guiding souls there. The Ley Lines of the Korolevskiy Theater had been modified by angels to make room for the souls of special creations, which hindered their ability to take ordinary souls: they could accept only two a day. Those killed by the Curse of Death were stuck in an afterlife that looked like the theater trapped in a blizzard.

Souls that die from the Curse of Death must return within a short window or miss their chance for good. Ronova said that the Ley Lines wanted back two long-lost souls, so each night they took an equal number to fill the gap. The Traveler and Mitya were able to help the two lost souls find clarity and "go to where they belong," which Mitya read as returning to the Ley Lines.

In 7.1 Mitya explains that because his soul bears Ronova's mark, he remembers everything that happens while he is dead, and that the recent theater incident showed a soul can be held briefly in the afterlife. He therefore proposes to do an experiment there. Vodyanitsa warns that the afterlife is Ronova's territory. Mitya also says he can sense the Curse of Immortality's signature on others.

Natlan night kingdom: When Natlan's people die they enter the Night Kingdom, a realm created by the Lord of the Night with Ronova's guidance that functions as Natlan's Ley Lines. There they eventually lose their sense of self and become one with the sea of souls. The souls in it are called Nightsouls, and Natlanese warriors draw on them for Nightsoul's Blessing.

Abyssal corrosion limited the Night Kingdom's capacity, so some souls were stuck in Natlan and would eventually and painfully disperse. If the soul had not been dead long and still held its form, a shaman of the Masters of the Night-Wind such as Citlali could "open the gate" for it, though the soul could refuse. These shamans can see Phlogiston and souls. Ancient Name bearers who fall in the Night Warden Wars can be raised by the Ode of Resurrection; a bearer who dies otherwise will eventually be reborn in Natlan in a different form. The Night Kingdom records only Natlanese memories.

The Weaver of Secrets, a Dragonlord, merged her consciousness into the Night Kingdom to create a "dream labyrinth" where the souls of deceased dragons and humans could rest in peace.

Natlan aftermath: After Capitano's sacrifice the Lord of the Night absorbed his life force and became essentially immortal, and souls from outside Natlan are now accepted into the Night Kingdom. Xbalanque, the first Pyro Archon, briefly returned to present-day Natlan in the body of a young boy, Mausau, because his own body could not be restored; he stayed one day.

Ghosts and echoes: Ghosts, also called spirits, appear throughout Teyvat. Flins, a Lightkeeper, says they are echoes of living souls: a portion of thoughts and memories that for certain reasons failed to enter the Ley Lines at death and so linger on the surface. They stay near fixed places and repeat words and phrases that mattered in life, and they are hard to reason with. In time their memories and yearning fade and slowly return to the Ley Lines.

The wiki lists ghosts in Mondstadt (Boreas), Liyue (Wuwang Hill, Mingyun Village), Inazuma (Tsurumi Island), Enkanomiya and Nod-Krai's Final Night Cemetery. Most keep their living appearance. The Shades of Tokoyo in Enkanomiya are projections of powerful emotions, the "Sins of Tokoyo," that look like featureless ghosts; one that realises it is a shade soon vanishes. Tsurumi's ghosts are featureless blobs, and it is unknown whether that is damage from the Ley Line Disorder there or a local belief. In Nod-Krai, Lightkeeper ghosts react strongly when the lighthouse is relit because it is deep in their memories.

Hanachirusato in Inazuma looks like a ghost but is a physical memory recreation of Kitsune Saiguu made by the Sacred Sakura from "filth" and is a different entity from the original. Flins stresses that the ghosts are but the memories of people that once were; those to whom they belonged are long gone. A Snezhnayan legend in Flins's lore describes Kyryll the Azure Flame as a blue flame that guided fallen souls across the icy plains.

Moons and irminsul: Diotima of Meropis, now in the Temple of Space, says she was once a boatman who sent wandering souls on silver ships to the Moon Capital above the clouds. In her time, three moons hung in the sky and each held Moon Envoys. Noble souls did not go to the ancient tree but followed the envoys to sleep eternally in cities on the moons. The wiki reads the Chanson of the Boatman, found in the Golden Hall, as suggesting this worked alongside Irminsul. Tsurumi's "Boatman" ghost is a similar figure, per the wiki.

When Zibai died protecting the civilization of Lang-Gan, Istaroth used the shadowmoon to preserve a portion of her soul. When the Frost Moon returned and the shadowmoon vanished, Zhongli and the Traveler reunited it with the other fragments in the Liyue Story Quest "A Lanternlit Ode to the Silver Moon" and restored her. Columbina split herself into three: body to moonlight poured over Nod-Krai (the origin of kuuvahki), soul left in the "moon's reflection" with a fragment anchoring her in a Luonnotar, and her Trilune Authority hidden in the Frost Moon.

Irminsul and the dead: In Version Luna VII, Nahida says a major problem arose within Irminsul because an intruder entered it through death, the one route she could not guard. She would not stop deceased souls from returning to the Ley Lines to guard against an invasion, because the souls of the departed must be allowed to find peace. Dottore, who was thought dead, is said by the wiki to have survived by planning his death so that half his soul would be recorded by Irminsul and the other half uploaded as data.

Aranara use "Sarva" for Irminsul and "return to Sarva" for passing away, which hints at an afterlife, though they also say they come from Sarva and travel through it, so its meaning is unsettled.

Soul stuff: A research note read in Ineffa's Character Story (6.0), written from Nephilheim's perspective, says a Moon Wheel, a ritual item given by the Three Moons to their followers so they could communicate, relies on a purer power (kuuvahki) than elemental energy and is "formed from the stuff of the soul." The same note says an acquired Vision sample, too, is soul-formed and wonders if Visions recently appeared alongside human wishes for that reason. Moon Wheels look like Nod-Krai Visions and allow Lunar Reactions.

This is an in-world researcher's hypothesis and partly redacted. The wiki's own comment is that Visions were probably formed from the same principle, with modern elemental energy in place of kuuvahki. Treat Visions as soul-linked only if the scene asks for that hypothesis.

Snegovik souls: Snowland fae such as the Snegovik, made for "companionship" with the people of Hyperborea, are incomplete in soul by nature: only by falling in love with a human and taking that person's soul can they become whole, according to texts cited by the wiki. Male Snegovik are knightly; female Snegurochka are mages. The Grand Duchess of the Snegurochka rules them from the House of Hesperides. Today they are among the most numerous fae in Snezhnaya.

Adepti and mortal souls: In Liyue, adepti arts include Dream Trawler, used to separate the soul from the body for self-cultivation and to summon another's spirit, as Xiao and the Traveler did with Starsnatcher. Pervases uses Mortal Lingering to regain a physical vessel temporarily. Mortals' souls are less robust, so prolonged contact with adepti, or a large infusion of adeptal energy, can overwhelm them, as it did with Qiqi.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Natlan characters use Nightsoul's Blessing, Nightsoul Points and Nightsoul Bursts, mechanics drawn from the Nightsouls of the Night Kingdom. Moon Wheel users in Nod-Krai trigger Lunar Reactions through Moonsign passives, built on kuuvahki. Ghost NPCs are quest and world features.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): keep soul talk regional. A Natlanese character thinks of the Night Kingdom and Nightsouls; a Nod-Krai Lightkeeper of ghosts and the Ley Lines; a Liyue adeptus of arts and parting. Do not blend them into a single universal rule.

Ghosts speak in fixed, repeated phrases about what mattered in life and rarely hold a conversation. A character who feels the dead near them should not claim certain knowledge about the afterlife. Ronova's account is her own claim.

Avoid presenting any one explanation as settled: whether souls are reincarnated, return to the Ley Lines, sleep on the moons or join a sea of souls depends on region and era. Do not give a living character the ability to see souls unless canon does, as it does for the Masters of the Night-Wind.

Limits: No source describes how reincarnation works, and no source lets an ordinary person talk to or free a soul at will.

A soul that has been dead too long or has lost its form is hard or impossible to help: in Natlan, dispersal is painful and unrecoverable, and in the Korolevskiy Theater, souls missing their window were lost for good.

Natlan's Night Kingdom recorded only Natlanese memories until Capitano's sacrifice; the Ode works only for Ancient Name bearers after a victory.

237.content: In Natlan, the dead enter the Night Kingdom, where they eventually lose their sense of self and join a sea of souls. Their remnants are the Nightsouls that warriors draw on for Nightsoul's Blessing. Abyssal corrosion limits the kingdom's capacity, and shamans such as Citlali can open the gate for a lingering soul, which may refuse to enter.

238.content: Flins describes ghosts as echoes of the living: portions of thoughts and memories that failed to enter the Ley Lines at death. They repeat phrases from life, stay near fixed places and may respond strongly to anything tied to their memories, like the relit lighthouse in Nod-Krai. In time they fade and return to the Ley Lines.

239.content: In an older age the noble dead were ferried by boatmen to cities on the moons, where they slept eternally. Diotima of Meropis, once such a boatman, now guides newcomers in the Temple of Space. The wiki reads another text as suggesting this ran alongside Irminsul.

240.content: In the Korolevskiy Theater, Ley Lines modified by angels accepted only two souls a day, so the cursed dead were stranded in an afterlife that felt like a blizzard. Ronova, who guided the souls, said a soul must return to the Ley Lines to complete death. Mitya, whose soul bears her mark, remembers what happens while he is dead.

241.content: Zibai's soul was divided into three fragments, one held in the shadowmoon by Istaroth, and was reunited by Zhongli and the Traveler. Columbina left part of her soul as an anchor in a Luonnotar when she split her being. Both are one-off, quest-specific cases.

242.content: Snegovik are said to be born with incomplete souls, made for companionship with humans in Hyperborea. They become whole only by falling in love with a human and taking that person's soul. This comes from texts the wiki cites, not a stated rule of the world.

243.content: A research note in Ineffa's Character Story calls the Moon Wheel "formed from the stuff of the soul," powered by kuuvahki rather than elemental energy, and suggests a Vision is similar. It is an in-world hypothesis, not confirmed canon.

244.content:
Spiritway (also: Spiritways, Spiritdoor, Spiritdoors): Spiritways are pathways of constantly flowing Phlogiston in Natlan. Anyone who can ride one moves swiftly in the direction of the flow. They first appeared in Version 5.0.

Only Koholasaurs, or people who have mastered the relevant technique, can use them freely, and the in-game text warns that not all Spiritways are complete or completely safe.

In universe: In-game text describes a Spiritway as a pathway formed by flowing Phlogiston. Riding it carries the traveller along the flow.

Spiritways may run one way or both ways; a route with portal-shaped ends is one-way, one without is bidirectional. A rider can join anywhere along the route and can leave at any point.

Modern Natlanese cannot simply make Spiritways. Their ancestors built Spiritdoors using Phlogiston Engraving, a technique that imitates the methods of those who made the Spiritways. A Spiritdoor, when interacted with, creates a Spiritway or makes an unstable one manifest. Canon does not name the original makers; see uncertainties.

Spiritways glow brighter and more vividly when the one riding is a People of the Springs character, Mavuika, or someone indwelling a Koholasaur, which suggests the flow responds to its rider.

Who can ride: A rider must be in the Nightsoul's Blessing state. The People of the Springs and Koholasaurs (through Saurian indwelling) can ride naturally. Mavuika is not of the People of the Springs; after a fourteenth round of modifications Xilonen made at her request, Mavuika's flamestrider gained the ability to manipulate Phlogiston and use Spiritways.

Leaving the Nightsoul's Blessing state, or ejecting from an indwelled Koholasaur, takes the rider off the Spiritway.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): riding a Spiritway consumes no Nightsoul points, Phlogiston or Stamina.

Collectibles and hazards appear along the route: Flowlight Orbs and Flowlight Targets to collect or break, and Flowlight Rifts to avoid. A rider can jump to dodge hazards, and Flowlight Leap carries them further.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present a Spiritway as a glowing current of Phlogiston that sweeps a rider along at speed, bright when a Natlanese traveller uses it. Do not let an ordinary visitor ride one without a Nightsoul-based method, and do not invent a Spiritway network or origins beyond what canon states.

245.content: Spiritdoors are devices made by the ancestors of modern Natlanese using Phlogiston Engraving to imitate the techniques of the Spiritway makers. Interacting with one creates a Spiritway or brings an unstable one into being.

246.content:
Spread (also: Spread reaction, Dendro Spread, Catalyze Spread): Spread is a Dendro elemental reaction. First, Dendro and Electro meet and make Quicken, which leaves a Quicken Aura on the target. Any later Dendro attack on that target then triggers Spread, which gives that attack a flat damage bonus. The Electro counterpart is Aggravate, and the Dendro bonus is the larger of the two.

It debuted in Version 3.0 with Quicken, Aggravate, Bloom, Burgeon and Hyperbloom, the reactions introduced for Dendro. Unlike many reactions, it does not deal damage of its own.

In universe: Canon gives no in-world explanation for Spread. The pages read treat it as a combat rule, so it is best understood as plant energy riding on lingering charge and spreading through a target.

A Sumeru preview teaser said the Electro and Dendro reaction has a deep connection to the history of Sumeru. Only that claim is on record; the wiki's connection to Rukkhadevata and Nabu Malikata is its own speculation.

Gameplay: Gameplay: Dendro on a target with a Quicken Aura triggers Spread and adds a bonus to the attack that triggered it. Spread does not use up the Quicken Aura.

- Spread is a catalyze reaction, with Quicken and Aggravate. It adds an Additive Base DMG Bonus to the attack, so the bonus enters the damage calculation before the attack's other bonuses, CRIT damage, DEF and resistance apply.
- The base bonus is 1.25 times a level multiplier for Spread, against 1.15 for Aggravate. The wiki notes that Dendro attacks therefore receive a greater bonus than Electro ones.
- Elemental Mastery and certain artifacts raise the reaction multiplier; the two sources add together.
- The Quicken Aura lasts a number of seconds equal to five times the smaller gauge of the two elements, plus six.

- Pyro or Hydro on a Quicken Aura use it up to trigger Burning or Bloom instead.
- For characters, the wiki's table of Spread base bonus values ends at level 90, while enemies and the environment have a value for level 100; the bonus rises steeply with level.
- The Dendro Elemental Resonance Sprawling Greenery in 3.0 gives nearby party members 20 Elemental Mastery for 6 seconds after Spread (or Aggravate, Burgeon, Hyperbloom), against 30 for Burning, Quicken or Bloom.

- The wiki lists talents that increase the Additive Base DMG Bonus from Spread; they are character-specific and not detailed here.
- Either element can start the Quicken Aura, but only Dendro attacks on it trigger Spread.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show green energy running along crackling sparks, a vine-like glow spreading across a target and feeding the next strike. The attack hits harder, but nothing explodes by itself.

It reads as a boost to one attack rather than a spectacle: the plant strike is sharpened by the current already on the target. Pair it with Quicken, so the lingering charge is visible first.

Avoid describing Spread as an area attack, as consuming the aura, or as something that happens without an Electro and Dendro pairing first. Do not link it to Sumeru's history as established fact.

Limits: Spread needs a Quicken Aura first and only Dendro triggers it. It has no damage of its own.

The Quicken Aura fades with time. Bloom or Burning can use it up if Hydro or Pyro is applied.

Examples: Gameplay example: an Electro attack lands on a Dendro-affected enemy and starts Quicken. The next Dendro attack triggers Spread and hits harder, and the aura stays for more Dendro hits.

247.content: Quicken is the starting reaction of the catalyze family: Dendro on an Electro-affected target, or the other way round. It deals no damage and leaves a Quicken Aura that fades over time. Dendro attacks on it trigger Spread, Electro ones trigger Aggravate, and neither consumes it. See system.quicken.

248.content:
Stamina (also: Stamina bar, stamina meter, maximum stamina): Stamina is the yellow bar that drains when you sprint, dash, climb, swim, glide or make a charged attack. It is one pool shared by the whole party, starts at 100 and regenerates quickly when you stop.

Upgrading the Statues of The Seven raises the maximum, up to 240.

In universe: Stamina is a game mechanic, not something characters mention by name. Gameplay abstraction: it represents the physical effort of running, climbing and swimming.

Gliding with a wind glider costs only 3 Stamina per second, far less than sprinting at 18.

Gameplay: Gameplay: stamina is a shared party pool shown as a yellow bar beside the active character. It regenerates at 25 per second after 1.5 seconds of not spending it, and the bar hides itself when full. Switching characters does not restore it.

The bar is divided into sections of 100 Stamina each. Base costs, before any reduction, include:
- Dash: 18 per movement; sprinting: 18 per second.
- Climbing: continuous cost not listed (5 Stamina is the minimum needed to begin); a climbing jump costs 25 per movement.
- Swimming: 4 per movement; swim dash: 2 to start, then about 10.2 per second.
- Gliding: 3 per second while moving.
- Charged attacks: most sword characters 20; polearm 25; most claymore 40 per second; most catalyst 50.
Many characters' passive talents, some Constellations and certain dishes reduce costs, remove them or restore stamina. The Stamina Flower restores 80 Stamina.

Maximum Stamina starts at 100. Each nation's Statues of The Seven can be upgraded with oculi; the maximum rises by 7 for each of the first two upgrades and 8 for the following seven, a total of +70 from one nation's statues at Level 10 (cumulative: Level 2 +7, 3 +14, 4 +22, 5 +30, 6 +38, 7 +46, 8 +54, 9 +62, 10 +70). The cap is 240, reachable with 18 upgrades across any two nations' statues or at least 19 upgrades spread across six nations. Statue Levels in a region are shared by all of that region's statues, and the stamina bonus is added until 240 is reached.
Reductions stack additively against the base cost: Impetuous Winds (two or more Anemo characters) takes 15% off; the wiki's example also uses Wolvensprint at 20%; a dish such as Barbatos Ratatouille takes 25%. In that example, sprinting drops from 18 to 7.2 per second. Total reduction is capped at about 92%. Anemograna cuts consumption by 30%. Condensed Ice (a Ley Line Disorder) raises consumption by 100% or 200%.

Other listed costs: Jean's Gale Blade hold, 20 per second; Keqing and Shikanoin Heizou, 25 for a charged attack; Tartaglia's Foul Legacy and the Raiden Shogun's Secret Art charged attacks and Arataki Itto, 20; Arlecchino's high-speed movement, 40 per second; Kinich and Mavuika, 50 for a charged attack. Ororon's and Citlali's mid-air Aiming Mode costs 75 for holding jump then 20 per second; the Alternate Sprint costs 10 to start then 15 per second. Two enemies, Abyss Herald: Frost Fall and Iniquitous Baptist, also have stamina costs listed for their frost attacks (50 and 80 respectively on first use).
Food that reduces sprint stamina costs applies to both dash and sprint; a second dish overrides the first, rather than stacking.

Limits: Gameplay: stamina cannot exceed the current maximum, does not regenerate until 1.5 seconds after you stop spending it, and is not restored by swapping characters. Costs differ by action and, for charged attacks, by weapon type.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): do not quote numbers in scene. Show effort through breathing, slowing pace, and hands slipping on a wall. Characters with stamina-related talents can be shown as lighter on their feet, but do not make them tireless.

249.comment: Stamina: Statue of The Seven stamina upgrades
249.content: Offering oculi at a nation's Statue of The Seven raises that nation's statue level, and each early level also adds to the party's maximum Stamina (7 for the first two upgrades, 8 for the next seven). The maximum possible is 240. See the Statue of The Seven entry for the offering mechanic itself.

250.content:
Statue of The Seven (also: Statues of The Seven, Archon statue, Archon statues, Statue of Seven): Statues of The Seven are large stone statues of each nation's Archon, found across Teyvat. Legends say they were sculpted in the image of The Seven who sustain the world, and travellers pray to them for protection. In play they unlock the map, act as teleport waypoints, heal and revive the party, and swap the Traveler's element.

Offering oculi to a nation's statues rewards the player and raises the party's maximum Stamina.

In universe: Mondstadt's statue honours the Anemo Archon, Liyue's the Geo Archon, Inazuma's the Electro Archon, Sumeru's the Dendro Archon, Fontaine's the Hydro Archon, Natlan's the Pyro Archon and Snezhnaya's the Cryo Archon. Each statue shows a hooded figure holding an object shaped like the region's Vision. The in-game map text calls them monumental statues that "watch over" the land.

Statues seem to depict the Archon currently in office. The game's description reads: "Legends say they were sculpted in the images of The Seven who sustain this world. Travelers would pray for the statue's protection should they come across one, while it silently anticipates the arrival of a noble soul."
According to fairytales cited in The Blessings of The Seven, the statues originally had gem eyes that swallows carried off. Item text on the Anemoculus describes offering consolidated winds to a statue so that it can regain power it has lost.

Areas that no Archon rules, such as Enkanomiya and the Golden Apple Archipelago, have no Statues of The Seven. Watatsumi Island was under Orobashi, not the Electro Archon, so it had none until Orobashi was slain; after that it gained a statue (a claim attributed to Mochizuki). Fontaine's statues match Focalors and Furina's Pneuma stance, not Egeria. Mondstadt also once lost a statue: the Traveler later finds a Defiled Statue hanging upside down in the ruins in Call of the Abyss. In Nod-Krai, the Frostmoon Scions built statues of Columbina called Statues of the New Moon.

Each nation's map text adds a motto. Mondstadt: "Seeds brought by the wind will grow over time". Liyue: its history is one of enduring stability. Inazuma: "Glory to the Shogun and her everlasting reign!" Sumeru: "There is nothing new under the sun." Fontaine: "The law is a fortress above all the waters of the world." Natlan: "Just as the perpetual living flame burns on without end, so too are struggle and change the true sovereigns of all things." Snezhnaya: "Only in the bitterest depths of winter does the steadfast pine reveal the warrior's resilience and unyielding strength."

Gameplay: Gameplay: each region's statues fill in map areas when first touched, unlock expeditions and teleport waypoints, revive fallen characters and heal the party. Interacting with a statue while playing the Traveler lets them change element to match that region.

Statue's Blessing: all statues share a pool of HP called Restorative Power. It refills at 1% of its maximum per 15 seconds (25 minutes for a full recharge). The maximum is 5,000 times the number of Statues of The Seven and Statues of the New Moon unlocked; the wiki gives 310,000 as the possible maximum as of Version 7.0 (55 statues of the Seven and 7 Statues of the New Moon). Each manual click heals a character by 10% of their maximum HP.
With "Auto-recover when nearby" enabled, fallen characters are revived at 35% HP for free, and party members below a chosen HP threshold are healed from the pool if you stay close for about 2 seconds. Statues also cleanse Bonds of Life and act as a source of warmth in Subzero Climate.

Oculi offerings: a nation's statues share a level. Offering the region's oculi gives Adventure EXP, Primogems and Sigils, and the first levels raise maximum Stamina (see the Stamina entry); Liyue statues also give Stones of Remembrance, and Inazuma, Sumeru, Fontaine and Snezhnaya statues give Shrines of Depths Keys and Memories. Natlan statues give Acquaint Fates. Snezhnaya's statues also let a player apply Cryo to enhance the Exaiphanes Blade. Natlan statues replenish Phlogiston where it is enabled.
First touch of a new statue gives 50 Adventure EXP and 5 Primogems. Mondstadt statues take 1 to 15 oculi per level; Liyue's take 2 to 30; Inazuma's take 10 to 30. Snezhnaya's take 20 to 32 across six levels. Switching back to Anemo, Paimon says, is done at a Mondstadt statue.
Only the Starfell Lake statue (during Bird's Eye View) and the Galesong Hill statue near Windrise are available at the very start. Others need obstacles cleared: a Windwail Highland statue guarded by an Eye of the Storm, a frozen statue on Dragonspine, and the Ochkanatlan statue (an activated switch).

Statue scenes with Paimon vary by region and story: she reacts to the Geo power at the first Liyue statue and to the light and humid air at the first Fontaine statue, and in Natlan she remarks that the statues feel odd compared with earlier nations'.
A statue grows more ornate as oculi are offered: broken stones are replaced at level 2, gold detail is added and cracks fixed at level 6, and a floating gold ring and Celestial-motif designs appear at level 10.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): statues are public landmarks where travellers rest, pray and wait for a safe teleport. Characters can say "pray to the statue" or "rest at the statue" without knowing about Restorative Power or oculi counts. Healing at a statue can be described as light and warmth rather than numbers.

Do not have an ordinary character explain the game's oculi or healing mechanics. Oculi are the exception: according to The Blessings of The Seven, only allogenes and the Traveler can see them, so an ordinary person would not be offering them.

251.comment: Statue of The Seven: Statues of the New Moon
251.content: In Nod-Krai, the Frostmoon Scions, who worship the Moon Goddess, built statues in the image of Columbina and placed them across the region, called Statues of the New Moon. They add to the Restorative Power pool like the Seven's statues in play.

252.comment: Statue of The Seven: Defiled Statue
252.content: Mondstadt long ago lost one of its Statues of The Seven. The Traveler later finds a Defiled Statue hanging upside down in the ruins in the quest Call of the Abyss.

253.content:
Stellar-Conduct (also: Stellar Conduct, Starlight Prism, Polestar Field): Stellar-Conduct is a Stellar Glimmer reaction from Snezhnaya. It happens when Cryo is applied to a target already affected by Electro, or the other way round, while a character with the matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party. It then replaces Superconduct. The reaction creates a Starlight Prism, which briefly turns the surrounding area into a Polestar Field.

It was added in Version Luna VIII (6.7), listed among the new systems of that version, and is the first of the two Stellar Glimmer reactions; Stellar Swirl followed in 7.0.

In universe: Canon says nothing in-world about the prism or the field. The only lore note concerns the whole family: Stellar Glimmer reactions are said to have been introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender, and the wiki cites a Version 7.0 livestream for that. Do not treat it as detailed history.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Stellar-Conduct does no damage by itself. Damage comes only from character talents and constellations, and may be Cryo or Electro depending on the source.

After the reaction, the Starlight Prism lasts 7 seconds and keeps a Polestar Field around it. Inside the field, Cryo and Electro hits on enemies are recorded by the Prism; the hit that created it does not count. Every 4 seconds the count is reset and buffs lasting 4 seconds are given. Characters inside the field gain a Cryo and Electro damage bonus (20%, or 28% plus 1% per recorded hit if any hit was recorded, up to 12 hits). Enemies in the field lose 40% Physical RES. The reaction's base coefficient rises by 40% plus 5% per recorded hit, up to 12 hits.

In the Snezhnayan open world, characters inside the field lose no heat and no Kresnik Energy, and Kresnik Energy under 30% is restored to 30%. Prime Ice Constructs and firearms get extra effects inside a Polestar Field. A Prism left over while the player is out of combat turns into a Prism Mirage after it expires. The player can activate it again, and it then lasts indefinitely, behaves like a Prime Ice Construct (placement limits, co-op construct, likes) and can be removed by interacting with it or from the map.

Version 7.0's Spiral Abyss gave one Blessing of the Abyssal Moon that made attacks inside a Polestar Field release a True DMG shockwave once every 4 seconds, and floor effects raised Stellar-Conduct damage by 50% and 75% in different halves. Version 7.0 also lowered the visual effects of the reaction at Low graphics settings. These are patch details, not canon.

Interactions: Stellar-Conduct replaces Superconduct when the matching passive is active, so Superconduct's usual outcome does not happen in that party. Stellar Swirl is the other Stellar Glimmer reaction.

Stellar Glimmer reactions also disable certain attacks of Snowland Fae and Aberrant Chimeric Monsters. The reaction deals damage only through talents and constellations; the wiki lists the talents, constellations, weapons and artifacts that enhance it.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show the Prism as a small star-like shard of light that hangs in the air above a frozen, crackling spot, with a faint ring of light around it. Allies inside it should feel steadier, and cold or heat should be easier to bear in Snezhnaya. Keep the scale at the size of a fight.

Do not treat Stellar-Conduct as something an ordinary Cryo or Electro Vision holder can do. It needs a Stellar Linchpin user, or the Cryo Traveler, present. Do not give it a made-up lore origin beyond what the family page says.

Limits: As of 7.1, no canon explains the reaction beyond its name and the family-level Saarelainen note.

Stellar-Conduct needs a Stellar Jubilee passive in the party. It is not a Lunar reaction.

254.comment: Stellar-Conduct: Starlight Prism and Polestar Field
254.content: The Starlight Prism is the object created by Stellar-Conduct. It lasts 7 seconds and sustains a Polestar Field, in which Cryo and Electro hits are recorded and then turned into party buffs. In the Snezhnayan open world, an unused Prism turns into a Prism Mirage that can be reactivated and then behaves like a Prime Ice Construct.

255.content:
Stellar Glimmer Reaction (also: Stellar Glimmer, Stellar Glimmer Reactions): Stellar Glimmer reactions are a small family of Cryo-related elemental reactions tied to Snezhnaya. There are two: Stellar-Conduct (Cryo with Electro) and Stellar Swirl (Anemo with Cryo). They take the place of Superconduct and Cryo Swirl only when a character with a matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party, and those characters are Stellar Linchpin users from Snezhnaya, or the Cryo Traveler.

The family was introduced in Version Luna VIII (6.7) with Stellar-Conduct, and Stellar Swirl followed in 7.0. Stellar Glimmer reactions also interrupt a specific attack from Snowland Fae and Aberrant Chimeric Monsters.

In universe: Canon gives the reactions almost no in-world explanation. The only lore note is that Stellar Glimmer reactions were introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender. The wiki sources this to the Version 7.0 Special Program livestream rather than to quest text.

Stellar Linchpins are Vision-like objects from Snezhnaya that let users manipulate the elements. Fatui research, as shown in the quest "Should We Meet Again", links them to the remains of Saarelainen. The Fatui's idea is that impurities from his remains become fixed in place when a Linchpin manifests, hence the name. Users of elemental energy through a Linchpin often show a power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat.

The Fatui want that otherworldly energy for Project Mistilteinn, a weapon meant to threaten the Heavenly Principles, which are used to fighting Light Realm energy and are the source of the Human Realm's elemental energy. Canon does not connect Mistilteinn to the Stellar Glimmer reactions directly. Do not claim that the reactions are the weapon.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a Stellar Glimmer reaction needs a character in the party with a passive talent that converts specific Cryo-related reactions. The two reactions are Stellar-Conduct, which replaces Superconduct, and Stellar Swirl, which replaces Cryo Swirl. The passives are called Stellar Jubilee passives.

Known Stellar Linchpin users are Sandrone (Cryo, 6.7), Odette (Cryo, 7.0), Vesna (Anemo, 7.1), Danica and Mitya (Electro, per the wiki's user list); the Cryo Traveler also has Stellar Jubilee passives. Artifacts, weapons and talents exist that raise Stellar Glimmer damage, and a Version 7.1 Spiral Abyss disorder boosts "Stellar Glimmer DMG" as a whole.

In the Spiral Abyss, Version 7.0 floors raised Stellar Swirl and Stellar-Conduct damage separately, and one Blessing of the Abyssal Moon rewarded attacks made inside a Polestar Field. These are event-style modifiers, not rules of the reactions themselves.

Enemies: Gameplay: Stellar Glimmer reactions disable certain attacks of Snowland Fae (Snegoviks, Vilas, Volkodlak Brutes) and Aberrant Chimeric Monsters, and a Leshy that is rooted and healing has its heart further exposed when a Stellar Glimmer reaction hits it.

The Snowland Fae are creatures of crystalline flesh from the biological alchemy of ancient Snezhnaya, as are the Aberrant Chimeric Monsters, which the wiki's text says were created under the Belyi Tsar. Canon does not explain why the Stellar reactions suit these creatures.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat these reactions as a Snezhnayan quirk of elemental power, visible in the company of a Linchpin user. Frost, static or wind react in an unusually bright, starlike way, with sparkling light and a sense of weight. Scale it to a skirmish: no Stellar reaction should be shown as a world-ending force.

A character who knows Snezhnayan lore might link the effect to the Third Descender, but ordinary people have no reason to. Do not make the reactions a secret Fatui project or a Mistilteinn component unless canon says so.

Limits: There are only two Stellar Glimmer reactions as of 7.1: Stellar-Conduct and Stellar Swirl. Do not invent further ones.

The reactions replace, not add to, the ordinary reactions, and require a Stellar Jubilee passive in the party. They are separate from the Lunar reactions, which depend on a Moonsign passive.

256.content:
A Stellar Linchpin is a Vision-like object from Snezhnaya that lets its user manipulate the elements. Fatui research connects Linchpins to the dead Third Descender, Saarelainen, whose remains left impurities that fix in place when a Linchpin forms. What makes one appear is unknown. Linchpin users are the ones who enable Stellar Glimmer reactions.

The wiki's user list names Sandrone, Odette, Vesna, Danica and Mitya. It adds that Aloy's Vision looks identical but is not established to be a Linchpin. Version 7.0 and 7.1 patch notes mention Mitya's element icon as the Electro Stellar Linchpin.

257.comment: Stellar Glimmer Reaction: Saarelainen and the reactions
257.content: The wiki records that Stellar Glimmer reactions were introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender, citing the 7.0 Special Program. Separately, Fatui research ties Stellar Linchpins to his remains. See the character entry for his history; this entry covers only the link to the reactions.

258.content:
Stellar Jubilee Passive (also: Stellar Jubilee, Stellar Jubilee Passives, Stellar Jubilee Passive Talent): A Stellar Jubilee Passive is a passive Talent held by characters with a Stellar Linchpin, plus the Cryo Traveler. It is what lets Stellar Glimmer reactions happen at all: with a holder in the party, the matching Cryo reactions turn into Snezhnayan Stellar Glimmer reactions. Sandrone, Odette and Vesna each have one, as does the Cryo Traveler.

This is a gameplay label, not a term used by characters in the story.

Gameplay: Gameplay, not literal lore. With a holder in the party, a Superconduct triggered by any party member becomes Stellar-Conduct, and a Cryo Swirl becomes Stellar Swirl. The passive also raises the base damage of the converted reaction in proportion to the holder's ATK, and puts the holder into a "Radiance" state.

- Radiance: Stellar-Conduct applies when the holder is inside a Polestar Field, the area a Stellar-Conduct creates around its Starlight Prism.
- Radiance: Stellar Swirl applies for 8 seconds after a nearby party member triggers Stellar Swirl.
- Sandrone (Light of Rationalisme), Odette (Dance of Aurore) and the Cryo Traveler (Illusory Frostmirror) convert both reactions. Vesna (Splendid Prelude) converts Cryo Swirl only.

- Bonus per 100 ATK: Sandrone and Odette add 0.7% base reaction damage, capped at 14%. The Cryo Traveler adds 0.35%, capped at 7%. Vesna adds 0.7% to Stellar Swirl, capped at 14%.
- A character can only be in one Radiance state at a time; where both could apply, Radiance: Stellar-Conduct takes priority (stated in Sandrone's separate talent text).
- The Radiance states make some skills deal their damage as Stellar-Conduct or Stellar Swirl damage, for example Vesna's Spirit Blades in Radiance: Stellar Swirl.

Stellar Glimmer reactions are a subset of elemental reactions that require a holder of a passive like this in the party. They also interrupt a particular attack of Snowland Fae and Aberrant Chimeric Monsters, and the Starlight Prism of a Stellar-Conduct matters in the Snezhnayan open world (see its own entry).

In universe: Gameplay abstraction; the story gives no in-world name for this passive. Canon context: Stellar Linchpins are Vision-like objects from Snezhnaya, and the Fatui's research ties them to the dead Third Descender, with users showing a power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat. In the Version 7.0 Special Program it was said that Stellar Glimmer reactions were introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen.

The Fatui seek the energy of Stellar Linchpins for Project Mistilteinn, a weapon against the Heavenly Principles (per the quest "Mistilteinn", as cited by the wiki). Why the Cryo Traveler can use the same reactions without a Linchpin is not explained in the pages read.

Holders: - Sandrone, Light of Rationalisme (released 6.7; the first holder, with Stellar-Conduct).
- Odette, Dance of Aurore (released 7.0).
- Vesna, Splendid Prelude (released 7.1).
- Traveler (Cryo), Illusory Frostmirror (version not verified).

The wiki's list of Stellar Linchpin users also names Danica and Mitya, who are not playable here, so they have no passive of this kind.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): treat the passive only as the reason that, around these characters, frost and lightning or frost and wind combine into a Snezhnayan star-like effect. Do not have characters name or discuss a "Stellar Jubilee Passive". Describe the result instead: a prism of light and a field of cold glittering light for Stellar-Conduct, a drifting vortex that bursts into frost for Stellar Swirl.

Limits: It enables only Stellar-Conduct (Cryo with Electro) and Stellar Swirl (Anemo with Cryo). Vesna's version covers Stellar Swirl alone. Do not extend it to other element pairs or to people without a Linchpin, apart from the Cryo Traveler.

259.content:
Stellar Linchpin (also: Stellar Linchpins, Linchpin, Snezhnayan star-Vision): A Stellar Linchpin is a Vision-like object from Snezhnaya. Like a Vision, it lets its bearer channel elemental power, but Stellar Linchpin users often show a kind of power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat. The Fatui believe Linchpins are tied to the remains of the Third Descender, and they study them for their weapon against the Heavenly Principles (Project Mistilteinn). Known users are Sandrone (Cryo), Odette (Cryo), Vesna (Anemo), Danica (Electro) and Mitya (Electro). Linchpin bearers can enable the Stellar Glimmer reactions.

It is not a Vision, a Gnosis or a Moon Wheel, and should not be called a Vision in narration. Sandrone, introducing the idea in 2026's Sunny Summer Fontinalia event (6.7), describes it as "a rare kind of Vision."

In universe: Visions are said to be a means of channelling elemental power for those who hold them. In Sandrone's explanation (as Marionette, in the 6.7 event), the same is true of Linchpins, with one difference: Linchpin users often exhibit a unique kind of power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat. What makes a Linchpin appear is not known.

Appearance in canon is gradual and personal. Sandrone found hers waiting on her workbench after her damaged body rebooted. Odette's formed in the "cold glimmer" backstage after a performance. Vesna's voice-over treats Linchpins as pretty collectible objects. Mitya wears his on a golden garter on the side of his left thigh, according to the wiki.

Sandrone says the Fatui work from the idea that Visions came from the same system that produced the Gnoses (themselves made from the Third Descender's remains), so a Vision's manifestation is also, to some extent, related to the Third Descender. Linchpins share that origin in stronger form. In Fatui research as Sandrone relays it, when a Linchpin manifests, impurities from the remains get fixed in place, which is where the name comes from and also what is thought to be the source of their strange power. This is Fatui belief, not something shown directly in the story.

Paimon and the Traveler had not heard of Linchpins before this conversation, though they already knew the remains of the Third Descender were used for the Gnoses. Sandrone is unsure whether the Linchpin has any lasting use for her: her character story has her deciding to use its Cryo as a cooling well for herself and her mechanism Fagio during heavy computing, and she is grateful that it set off Alain's gift, her second life.

The third descender link: In Fatui research as relayed by Sandrone (Marionette), Stellar Linchpins are related to the Third Descender. When one manifests, impurities from his remains get fixed in place. In canon, the Heavenly Principles used his remains to create the seven Gnoses, which consolidated the Archon system; Visions come from that same system.

The Third Descender's name is Saarelainen, and the wiki credits the introduction of Stellar Glimmer reactions to ancient Snezhnaya to him. Treat the Linchpin link as a belief of Snezhnayan researchers and some in-world voices, not a proven mechanism.

Origins in users: How each known user got a Linchpin, as the sources tell it:
- Sandrone: she was badly damaged in a fight with Il Dottore, and a Linchpin appeared and activated a built-in "Final Gift" left by her creator Alain Guillotin, a second chance for a body that would otherwise have shut down. After her core rebooted, she repaired herself and imported her old numerological array and some surviving algorithms from Pulonia, who was beyond repair. She says she has no idea why it appeared for her.
- Odette: in her character story she had trained until she felt no pain and, after a performance, found an ice-blue crystal forming in the cold glimmer backstage. She recognises it as a Linchpin from what she heard among the Fatui, and accepts it. In her voice-over she describes waking from near-unconsciousness with frostbite and seeing a light from a Linchpin in front of her, and wonders whether it was her will to survive that woke her.
- Vesna: her "Stellar Linchpin" character story is about the death of her teacher, the Captain, and her grief; the text I reviewed does not say how her Linchpin came to her.
- Danica and Mitya: wiki infoboxes list Linchpins as their element source (Electro for both). Mitya also reverse-engineered Linchpin energy for Project Mistilteinn.

Sandrone's story also says the Linchpin was necessary for the gift to trigger: the damage to her core was too severe, and without it the gift would not have fired. She says it was almost wasted on the fight with Dottore.

Project mistilteinn: Pierro of the Fatui explains in the Archon Quest "Wraith's Nocturne" (Act II, "Mistilteinn", 7.0) that elemental energy is the Human Realm's power, converted by the Heavenly Principles themselves, so using it against its creator would be futile. The Fatui therefore turned to the energy associated with the Third Descender and the Linchpins. By reverse-engineering Linchpins to extract their energy, they have what Pierro calls a source of "anti-Celestia energy."

The wiki describes Project Mistilteinn as a weapon allowing the Tsaritsa to fight the Heavenly Principles, overseen by Pierro and the Armory Palace, with Project Stuzha regulating Snezhnaya's energy consumption to feed it. Mitya, a scientist of the Royal Energy Commission of Snezhnaya, is the one in charge of energy research and the extraction of Linchpin energy into Anti-Celestia Energy.

Appearance: A Stellar Linchpin is shaped like a four-pointed star, similar to the shape of a Primogem, set in a star-shaped frame. Its casing resembles a Snezhnayan Vision's, with two rhombuses beneath the star. Mitya's is Electro and sits on his left thigh; Odette's was described as ice-blue, cold and almost weightless, no heavier than a frozen tear.

Aloy's Vision has a similar four-pointed star in a gold circular frame, but the wiki says it is not established as a Stellar Linchpin and works like a normal Vision. Vesna's voice-over calls Linchpins "beautifully designed" and "absolutely a collector's item," adding that Moon Wheels aren't bad either and that she is not interested in Visions at the moment.

Known users: Sandrone (Cryo), Odette (Cryo), Vesna (Anemo), Danica (Electro), Mitya (Electro).

- Sandrone: Seventh of the Eleven Fatui Harbingers, artificer; her Linchpin appeared in the 6.7 event.
- Odette: prima ballerina of the Korolevskiy Troupe, Fatui; released 7.0.
- Vesna: Commander-in-chief of the Druzhna; Anemo user, released 7.1.
- Danica: head housemaid of the royal house.
- Mitya: scientist of the Royal Energy Commission.
Their personal stories belong to their own entries.

Linchpin users appear mostly in Snezhnayan service: the Fatui, the Druzhna, the royal household and its research organisations. Sandrone, Odette and the Traveler (Cryo) are the Cryo set. Vesna is the Anemo user, and the Electro users Danica and Mitya appear in the Archon Quest (Mitya is named a Linchpin user in the 7.0 known-issues note).

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Characters with a Linchpin have a Stellar Jubilee Passive, which lets them enable Stellar Glimmer reactions. The Traveler (Cryo) has them too.

Stellar-Conduct (Superconduct converted; introduced 6.7 with Sandrone) is enabled by Sandrone and Odette. Stellar Swirl (Cryo Swirl converted; introduced 7.0) is enabled by Odette and Vesna. Stellar Glimmer reactions are a subset of elemental reactions. A talent that converts the matching Cryo-related reaction must be present in the party. The wiki credits ancient Snezhnaya as the setting where Saarelainen introduced these reactions.

Limits: A Stellar Linchpin is not a Vision, and is not a substitute for a Gnosis. Sandrone herself uses it modestly: it supplies Cryo, which she uses to cool her systems, and she does not find that it solves problems for her. No canon text says a Linchpin makes its holder more than a skilled Vision-like elemental user.

Linchpins are said to carry a power from beyond Teyvat, yet no source quantifies it. The Fatui treat them as raw material for the anti-Celestia energy that is meant to threaten the Heavenly Principles, but whether Mistilteinn works is not shown as of 7.1.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): describe the Linchpin as a small, cold-looking star carried on the body like a Vision. Do not have an ordinary bystander name it correctly; it is a Snezhnayan matter, and Paimon needed Sandrone to explain it.

Characters who know Fatui research may mention the Third Descender link, but should treat it as theory. Let users react personally: Sandrone with dry practicality, Odette with quiet acceptance, Vesna with an aesthete's curiosity.

Avoid inventing wishes that "caused" a Linchpin for a character whose story does not say so, and avoid giving other nations' Vision holders a Linchpin.

260.comment: Stellar Linchpin: Stellar Linchpin and the Third Descender
260.content: Fatui research says Linchpins relate to the Third Descender, whose remains the Heavenly Principles used to make the seven Gnoses. When one manifests, impurities from the remains get fixed in place, explaining the name and the strange power. Treat as Fatui belief.

261.content: Gameplay: the passive talent shared by Stellar Linchpin users (and the Traveler as Cryo) that enables Stellar Glimmer reactions. Stellar-Conduct arrived in 6.7 and Stellar Swirl in 7.0.

262.content: Pierro's name for the energy obtained by reverse-engineering Stellar Linchpins. Mitya extracted it for Project Mistilteinn, the Fatui weapon aimed at the Heavenly Principles. It is meant to succeed where ordinary elemental energy would not.

263.comment: Stellar Linchpin: Should We Meet Again
263.content: During the limited-time event "Sunny Summer Fontinalia" (6.7), Sandrone in her Marionette guise, aboard a rented ship near Fontaine, explained Stellar Linchpins and her Final Gift to Paimon and the Traveler while seeking Alain's underwater home.

264.content:
Stellar Swirl (also: Stellar Vortex): Stellar Swirl is a Stellar Glimmer reaction from Snezhnaya. It happens when Anemo is applied to a target already affected by Cryo, while a character with the matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party. It then replaces Cryo Swirl. It deals Anemo damage and leaves a Stellar Vortex that later bursts for Cryo damage.

It was added in Version 7.0 ("Everwinter Without Mercy"), after Stellar-Conduct in 6.7. The announcement presented it as a reaction that disturbs opponents and also helps exploration.

In universe: Canon says nothing in-world about the vortex. The only lore note concerns the family: Stellar Glimmer reactions are said to have been introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender, citing a 7.0 livestream.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): on triggering, one hit of Anemo damage is dealt to the target, and a Level 1 Stellar Vortex appears for 3 seconds. After a delay the vortex bursts, dealing area Cryo damage.

Triggering Stellar Swirl a third time raises the vortex to Level 2, so that it bursts for more damage over a wider area. Three further triggers make it burst at once. For 5 seconds after any vortex bursts, the player's next jump is higher, which the announcement framed as an exploration aid.

The Version 7.1 patch notes fixed an error where the reaction's damage could leave out Cryo characters involved in the reaction. Spiral Abyss floors in 7.0 raised Stellar Swirl damage by 50% and, in the later phase, by 75% in one half, and one blessing created a True DMG shockwave from Swirl or Stellar Swirl damage once every 4 seconds. These are patch details, not canon.

Interactions: Stellar Swirl replaces Cryo Swirl in a party with a matching passive, so Anemo on a Cryo target no longer spreads Cryo to nearby targets. It does not replace Swirl with Pyro, Hydro or Electro. Stellar-Conduct is the other Stellar Glimmer reaction.

Stellar Glimmer reactions also disable certain attacks of Snowland Fae and Aberrant Chimeric Monsters. Known Stellar Linchpin users include Vesna, the Anemo user introduced in 7.1; Odette in 7.0 is a Cryo user.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Stellar Swirl as a small, bright whirl of frost and starlight that spins in place for a breath before it bursts outward. Anemo moves it, Cryo is what it leaves behind. Keep it to skirmish scale.

Do not describe it as an ordinary Anemo Vision holder's Swirl. It needs a Stellar Linchpin user, or the Cryo Traveler, to be present. Do not invent a lore origin beyond the family note.

Limits: As of 7.1, no canon explains the reaction beyond its name and the family-level Saarelainen note.

Stellar Swirl needs a Stellar Jubilee passive in the party and an Anemo-Cryo pairing. It does not apply to other elements and is not a Lunar reaction.

History note: The Hoyolab announcement for 7.0 described Stellar Swirl as following Stellar-Conduct, introduced in Version Luna VIII, and listed its features as the vortex, disrupting opponents, and supporting exploration. It also noted a Starlight Prism effect that provides warmth and enhances constructs, which belongs to Stellar-Conduct's own entry.

265.content: The Stellar Vortex is the object left by Stellar Swirl. It lasts 3 seconds, bursts for area Cryo damage, levels up with repeated triggers, and boosts the next jump after it bursts.

266.content:
Superconduct (also: Superconduct reaction, Electro-Cryo reaction): Superconduct is the reaction that happens when Electro meets Cryo on a target, in either order. It is a burst of Cryo energy that damages everything in a small area and strips Physical resistance from the enemies it touches, so that sword, spear and fist hurt more for a while. It is a combat rule rather than a story event.

The damage is fixed by the reaction itself (the level and Elemental Mastery of whoever triggers it), not by the attack that set it off. The Cryo is not left on the target, so Superconduct cannot lead to a second reaction.

In universe: Canon does not explain Superconduct as a phenomenon of the world; it is introduced only through the game's Elemental Trial tutorial. Treat any in-world explanation as a scene decision, not as lore.

Outside battle the game shows the same pairing in the environment. Electro on water that Cryo has frozen shortens the freeze and leaves the water Electro-Charged, without area damage or Physical RES loss. Cryo on an Electro Crystal, or Electro on a Mist Flower, triggers a full Superconduct and hurts enemies nearby.

Version 7.0 added Stellar-Conduct, a Stellar Glimmer reaction that replaces Superconduct when a character with a matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party. The wiki credits the introduction of Stellar Glimmer reactions to ancient Snezhnaya, through Saarelainen, citing the 7.0 Special Program. Ordinary Superconduct is unchanged outside that condition.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Superconduct deals AoE Cryo damage in a 5 m radius and reduces the Physical RES of enemies in the area by 40% for 12 seconds.

It is a transformative reaction with base coefficient 1.5 (from the wiki's Damage page), scaled by the triggering character's level and Elemental Mastery. It ignores the attack's ATK and cannot CRIT by default. Target resistance applies; DEF is practically ignored. Only the party applying the second element counts.

Electro on a Frozen target triggers Superconduct and consumes the Freeze. One target can take at most 2 instances of Superconduct damage every 0.5 seconds from the same attacker, and several Superconducts on the same target within 0.1 seconds deal damage only once. Talents, constellations and artifact sets exist that raise Superconduct damage.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Superconduct as a sharp crack of frost and static, a ring of shards or a snap of ice-blue lightning, followed by armour, hides or bone visibly weakening. Describe the effect as a short-lived weakness to blows, not a permanent wound.

Because the damage is Cryo and the lasting benefit is Physical, narrate it as setting up the next strike. Do not claim Superconduct leaves lingering frost on the target; the reaction does not.

Limits: Superconduct needs both Electro and Cryo; no other element pair produces it.

It applies no Cryo, so it cannot chain into Frozen, Melt or another Cryo reaction. Cryo on Electro-Charged water does not trigger it in the environment.

The Physical RES reduction applies to enemies in the burst, not to the reaction's source. Under the Stellar-Conduct conditions (7.0) the reaction becomes a different one.

267.content:
Superconduct is the Electro and Cryo reaction. It bursts with Cryo damage in a 5 m radius and lowers Physical RES by 40% for 12 seconds for enemies in the area. It leaves no Cryo behind.

Environmental forms: Electro on frozen water shortens the freeze and electrifies the water without area damage or Physical RES loss, while Cryo on an Electro Crystal or Electro on a Mist Flower triggers a full Superconduct. In 7.0, Stellar-Conduct can replace it if a character with the matching passive is in the party.

268.content:
Swirl (also: Swirl reaction, Anemo Swirl, Pyro Swirl, Hydro Swirl, Electro Swirl, Cryo Swirl): Swirl is what happens when Anemo meets another element on a target: the wind catches that element and flings it outward, so everything nearby is hit or soaked with it. It works with Pyro, Hydro, Electro and Cryo, but not with Geo or Dendro. It is a combat rule rather than a story event.

Swirl deals its own damage in the swirled element (except Hydro, which only spreads Wet), based on the Anemo user's level and Elemental Mastery rather than ATK. Because it re-applies the element, it can set off further reactions on neighbouring targets.

In universe: Canon presents Swirl only through the Elemental Trial tutorial and gameplay text; no source read gives an in-world account of why wind spreads elements. Treat any explanation as a scene decision.

The tutorial wording is that when Anemo touches Hydro, Pyro, Cryo or Electro, the element in contact affects a larger area and can trigger other reactions.

Version 7.0 introduced Stellar Swirl, a Stellar Glimmer reaction that replaces Cryo Swirl when a character with a matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party. Ordinary Cryo Swirl is unchanged outside that condition (see its own entry).

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Swirl applies the non-Anemo element to targets within a 6 m radius, except the target the reaction was triggered on. Pyro, Electro and Cryo Swirl also deal AoE damage of that element; Hydro Swirl spreads Wet and deals damage only to the triggering target.

It is a transformative reaction with base coefficient 0.6 (from the wiki's Damage page), scaled by the Anemo character's level and Elemental Mastery. It cannot CRIT by default and ignores ATK. The wiki separates this from Elemental Absorption, where an Anemo skill absorbs an element and deals ordinary damage of it; that damage uses normal attack stats.

Secondary reactions caused by a Swirl take their damage from the Anemo user: swirled Pyro onto an Electro target triggers Overloaded using the Anemo character's level and EM, and swirl-induced Melt, Vaporize or Aggravate are likewise scaled by them. One target takes at most 2 Swirl instances every 0.5 seconds from the same attacker, and several Swirls of one element on a target within 0.1 seconds count once, with limits separate for each swirled element.

Players cannot apply a lasting Anemo aura, so Swirl is normally triggered by an Anemo attack landing on a target already affected by another element. The one exception noted on the wiki is the Anemo Hypostasis, which keeps Anemo on itself while its core is exposed. An Anemo hit on a Frozen target consumes the Freeze to trigger Swirl.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Swirl as a gust that grabs the burning, dripping, crackling or frosted thing and throws it out in a ring, with a scatter of sparks, spray or frost. The wind should visibly carry the element.

Hydro Swirl is the gentlest form: spray and dampness that leaves neighbours Wet, with no burst. Do not have the wind create an element that was not already present on the target.

Limits: Swirl does not work with Geo or Dendro, and Anemo has no reaction with itself.

It spreads an element already present; it does not create one. The swirled element is not applied back to the triggering target, which lets the original target keep its own state.

Hydro Swirl does no area damage. Swirl damage is unaffected by ATK, CRIT or general damage bonuses; only Swirl-specific bonuses raise it.

269.content:
Swirl is the Anemo reaction with Pyro, Hydro, Electro or Cryo. It spreads that element to everything within 6 m of the target and deals the element's damage (Hydro only spreads Wet).

It scales with the Anemo character's level and Elemental Mastery, and secondary reactions it causes borrow those stats. In 7.0, Stellar Swirl can replace Cryo Swirl when the matching passive is in the party.

270.content:
Talent (also: Talents, character talents, Combat Talents, Passive Talents, Ascension Passive): "Talents" is the game's interface term for the abilities of a playable character. Most characters have three Combat Talents (Normal Attack, Elemental Skill, Elemental Burst), two Ascension Passives and one Utility Passive. It is a gameplay abstraction: in the story people simply use their powers, skills or arts. Never have a character say "my Talent level is 9".

Talents are sorted into Combat, Ascension and Passive types. Some characters also carry extra passives tied to later systems (Natlan, Nod-Krai, Snezhnaya and Hexerei content).

In universe: Nothing found shows canon using "Talents" as an in-world category. What the interface lists as Talents are, in the story, a character's fighting style, Vision or Authority power, trained techniques and personal knacks.

The one Talent-adjacent idea with real lore is the Constellation: star signs said to govern the fates of Teyvat's people, whose unlocks upgrade a character's abilities in the game. Their lore and mechanics belong to the Constellation entry; here they matter only because two of them raise Combat Talent levels.

Combat talents: Every character starts with three Combat Talents unlocked at level 1: the Normal Attack (their main attack form), the Elemental Skill (no Energy cost, but a cooldown) and the Elemental Burst (usually costs Energy).

Combat Talent levels rise by spending Character Talent Materials ("talent books", from the weekday Domains of Mastery of each nation) up to level 10, with the usable cap set by the character's Ascension phase. Talent levelling starts at Ascension phase 2 (around character level 40 and Adventure Rank 25).

- The third and fifth Constellations each raise one specific Combat Talent by 3 levels and lift that Talent's cap from 10 to 15. Materials alone cannot go beyond level 10; the final steps to 15 need other effects.
- Some passive Talents raise the level of a category of Talent.
- During certain events, items or Stratagems temporarily raise Skill or Burst levels inside a domain.
- Values scale by a multiplier per Talent level. For most percentage values level 10 is 180% of the base, and Normal Attacks scale slightly differently. Exceptions exist, such as Xiao's and Zhongli's Bursts, which follow their own scaling.
- Talents hit the selected enemy by default, and otherwise the area in front of the character.

- Percentage values and flat values scale on different multipliers. A flat value at level 10 is 220% of the base, against 180% for percentages; the Normal Attack multiplier at level 10 is 197.5%.
- Stat effects from most passives are not shown on the Combat Talent screens, even when unconditional. The exception is Witch's Eve Rite and Witch's Revelation passives that give a Combat Talent its own buff tab.
- Alternate Sprints cannot be jumped from, may snag on stairs or rocks, and are not helped by stamina-reduction effects.

Ascension passives: Two passive Talents unlock with Ascension: the 1st Ascension Passive (phase 1, character level 20) and the 4th Ascension Passive (phase 4). Most improve a Combat Talent.

Ascension Passives cannot be levelled up. Their effects often do not show on the Combat Talent's own attribute screen.

Passive talents: Besides Ascension Passives, a character has a Utility Passive (also called an Exploration Talent), unlocked on acquisition; the Traveler has none. It does something outside combat: cooking, crafting or forging bonuses, reduced stamina cost, faster movement, expedition bonuses, resource markers on the map, or not startling certain wildlife.

Alternate Sprints replace normal sprinting and are listed as an additional passive. They cost 10 Stamina to start and 15 per second afterwards, against 18 and 18 for a normal sprint; they cannot be levelled.

Special passive categories, each limited to characters tied to a system:
- Night Realm's Gift: Natlan characters, tied to Nightsoul's Blessing and Phlogiston.
- Moonsign Benediction: Nod-Krai characters and Zibai; each raises the party's Moonsign level by 1, and Columbina's and Moon Wheel users' versions also enable Lunar Reactions.
- Stellar Jubilee: Snezhnaya characters with Stellar Linchpins and the Cryo Traveler, enabling Stellar Glimmer Reactions.
- Witch's Eve Rite: Hexerei characters, unlocked by completing their Witch's Homework quest (character level 70 or above). Most effects need at least two Hexerei characters in the party.
- Witch's Revelation: certain characters, unlocked through a Witch's Revelation quest, also at level 70 or above. It enhances Talents and Constellations and lets the character enter a Radiance state inside a Polestar Field.

Gameplay: Gameplay (labelled mechanics, not lore): the Normal Attack, Skill and Burst buttons use the matching Talent, and an Alternate Sprint is used if the character has one. Talents largely decide a character's role in a team; Elemental Resonance and other team bonuses sit on top of Talents rather than inside them.

Limits: Do not give a character a numeric Talent level, a cooldown readout or an Energy bar in dialogue, and do not call story powers "Talents".

Talents are not Visions or Constellations. A Vision (or Authority) is the source of an element, while Talents are what a character does with it. The Traveler has no Utility Passive.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon): describe Talents through their fiction, such as a signature move, a technique that needs a pause before reuse (the cooldown), or a finishing move that drains the user (the Burst). A passive can show as a habit or knack. Stay with what canon shows the character doing.

271.content: A Combat Talent starts at level 1 and rises to level 10 with Character Talent Materials, limited by Ascension phase. Constellations that raise a Talent by 3 levels lift its cap to 15.

272.content: Each character apart from the Traveler has a Utility Passive from the start, giving a non-combat benefit such as a crafting refund, a stamina reduction, a movement bonus or map markers.

273.content:
Teleport Waypoint (also: Teleport Waypoints, Portable Waypoint, Sub-Space Waypoint, fast travel): Teleport Waypoints are devices found across Teyvat. Once the Traveler unlocks one by touching it, it can be chosen on the map to fast travel there. In-world, they are old, odd structures the locals have grown used to without knowing what they are for; to the Traveler, a foreigner, their use is obvious.

The map text puts it this way: Teyvat's people regard them as ancient gimmicks and are accustomed to them despite not knowing their purpose.

In universe: Canon gives no explanation of who built Teleport Waypoints or how they work. Treat them as unexplained ancient machinery that happens to carry the Traveler between places.

The Portable Waypoint's item text offers a different note: it describes a pocket-sized item that makes a temporary Waypoint, able to connect with the ley lines at least enough to bring about teleportation, and adds that the real principles behind Waypoints are not yet fully understood and that the hope is that using them has no undesirable side effects. That text speaks from inside the world and treats the Waypoints as known devices, which does not match the "ancient gimmick nobody understands" framing.

Other teleportation exists in canon but is not shown to be the same thing: Mona uses a teleport in the event Unreconciled Stars, the Fatui appear to teleport in Archon Quest Chapter I, Act III, and a Fatui knight remarks that the Grand Master crossed from Nod-Krai to Mondstadt along the ley lines. In the Archon Quest "In the Depths, an Unexpected Reunion" Paimon likens Dainsleif's description of the Abyss's portal network to Teleport Waypoints, which the story does not develop. The wiki marks the canonicity of Waypoints as unclear.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Waypoints are map markers that are unlocked by interacting with them, then used to fast travel. Statues of The Seven, Statues of the New Moon, domains and High-Speed Transit Lanes also work as teleport points once unlocked.

They also act as respawn points when a whole party falls, clear accumulated Sheer Cold, Withering decay and Abyssal decay from harmful climates, recharge the Lumenstone Adjuvant in The Chasm: Underground Mines, and replenish Phlogiston in Natlan. Most are unlocked by touching them once the area is lit up on the map, which is done through a Statue of The Seven or Statue of the New Moon, or through quest progress.

Some Waypoints are hidden until a requirement is met, usually quest progress. Examples include those inside the Dainichi Mikoshi in Enkanomiya, the underground ones in Sumeru's deserts, those in Annapausis and the Fortress of Meropide in Fontaine, and sites in Chenyu Vale. Certain map locations also act as teleport points after set quest steps, among them the Alcor, the Cat's Tail, the Fortress of Meropide, the Hidden Dwelling and the Meeting Points in Nod-Krai (after the opening Nod-Krai quest "Where the Moon Rises" and each Meeting Point's own world quest). Several Waypoints are unlocked automatically on completing the Archon Quest "Song of the Dragon and Freedom". Co-op: a fallen player respawns at the nearest Waypoint they have unlocked in their own world.

Variants: the Portable Waypoint is crafted by alchemy, with the instructions earned at Mondstadt Reputation Level 6, and creates a single temporary Waypoint that lasts seven days, which guests in co-op can use. Sub-Space Waypoints are furnishings placed in the Serenitea Pot. The Realm Waypoint "A Place to Return To" sits in the first area of each realm layout.

Limited event waypoints: Event-only areas have had their own Waypoints that can no longer be reached: 7 in the Golden Apple Archipelago during the 1.6 event Midsummer Island Adventure, and 10 when it returned in 2.8; 10 in the Darkness-Encroached Enkanomiya in 2.5; 9 in the Veluriyam Mirage in 3.8; and 17 in Simulanka in 4.8. Some were unlocked automatically during the event quests or once the event ended.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): inside a scene, the Traveler stepping onto a Waypoint and arriving elsewhere is fine as a shorthand for travel. Locals treat the devices as familiar background furniture, not as technology anyone can explain. Do not claim Waypoints run on ley lines, belong to a particular civilisation, or that ordinary NPCs can use them, as canon supports none of these.

Limits: Canon gives no builder, no mechanism and no in-world rules. Katheryne's fast-travel remark in Inazuma is not a basis for treating other characters as able to teleport. Fast travel is a gameplay convenience; most Fatui, Knights and travellers are shown crossing Teyvat on foot, by ship or by other means.

274.content: The Portable Waypoint is an alchemy-made consumable that creates one temporary Teleport Waypoint at the user's location. It lasts seven days and only one can exist per world. Its item text calls it a pocket-sized item capable of connecting with the ley lines enough to cause teleportation, and notes that its convenience for Vision bearers comes with the caveat that the real principles of Waypoints are not fully understood. Sub-Space Waypoints are furnishings for the Serenitea Pot that look different but work the same way.

275.content:
Vaporize (also: Vaporize reaction, Pyro-Hydro reaction): Vaporize is what happens when Pyro and Hydro meet on a target. It deals no damage by itself; instead the attack that triggers it hits much harder, as if the water flashed to steam under the blow. It is a combat rule rather than a story event.

Which element lands second decides the strength: a Hydro hit on a Pyro-affected target is amplified more than a Pyro hit on a Hydro-affected target.

In universe: Canon presents Vaporize only through the Elemental Trial tutorial and gameplay text. No source read for this entry gives an in-world account of why it amplifies damage, so any in-world explanation is a scene decision.

The tutorial wording is simply that when Pyro meets Hydro, the triggering Hydro or Pyro damage receives a bonus, and that the bonus is larger when Hydro is the trigger.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Vaporize multiplies the damage of the triggering attack by 2 if Hydro is applied to a Pyro-affected target, and by 1.5 if Pyro is applied to a Hydro-affected target.

It is an amplifying reaction, like Melt. The multiplier is further increased by a percentage based on the triggering character's Elemental Mastery plus any Reaction DMG Bonus from effects such as artifact sets. Vaporize deals no damage of its own, so a talent that only applies an element and deals no damage gains nothing from it.

The 1.5x ("reverse") form consumes less of the original element than the 2x ("forward") form, so it often leaves part of the aura in place. Talents, constellations and artifact sets exist that raise Vaporize damage, and the multiplier can also apply to damage from separate reaction instances, not only direct attacks.

The wiki gives the multiplier as the base coefficient (2.0 for Hydro triggering, 1.5 for Pyro triggering) times one plus the Elemental Mastery bonus and any Reaction DMG Bonus, with the Elemental Mastery bonus approximated as 2.78 x EM / (EM + 1400). It multiplies the damage before the reaction is otherwise accounted for.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show Vaporize as a burst of hissing steam when water strikes fire, or when flame scorches a wet foe, followed by a visibly harder hit. Keep it about the force of the blow, not extra effects.

Water on flame, the stronger case, can be narrated as the more dramatic hit. Do not treat the steam as a lingering cloud or a status on the target; canon describes none.

Limits: Vaporize needs both Pyro and Hydro, and it never creates damage on its own.

It does not turn into another reaction and does not involve Geo, Anemo, Electro, Cryo or Dendro.

276.content:
Vaporize is the Pyro and Hydro reaction. It amplifies the triggering hit: x2 when Hydro triggers it, x1.5 when Pyro does. It deals no damage of its own.

Elemental Mastery adds a further percentage to the multiplier, and certain talents, constellations and artifact sets improve it. The sibling reaction for Pyro and Cryo is Melt.

277.content:
Vision (also: Visions, God's Eye, Eye of God, allogene, allogenes): A Vision is a jeweled amulet, worn on the body, that lets its bearer channel one of the seven elements directly. The bearers are called allogenes: people with unusually strong desires or ambitions who might one day ascend to Celestia and become gods. Most people never receive one. A Vision does not give mastery, only the channel; the power still has to be practised.

Common belief says the Archons hand Visions out, but canon states they do not pick recipients and do not know who receives them. Visions are given as a form of acknowledgement by Celestia, and they cannot be destroyed.
